items.title: Unilorin student seeks N43m for kidney transplant
items.description: … Family spends over N20m, sells property to sustain treatment By Chioma Obinna The family of Olajide Victor, a 200-level student of the University of Ilorin, Kwara State, has appealed for N43 million to fund a kidney transplant for him after he was diagnosed with Stage V end-stage renal disease. Victor is expected to undergo the life-saving procedure at Newhaven Specialist Hospital, Lagos, as his family struggles to meet the cost of his treatment. He said his health challenges began in November 2025 after he sustained a minor fracture in his left leg while playing football at the university’s sports complex. Weeks later, his face and legs became swollen, prompting medical examinations. Following several tests, including kidney function investigations, he was diagnosed with Stage V kidney disease at Taiwo Hospital, Ilorin. A medical report signed by Dr S. Alagbe, Consultant Nephrologist, indicated that Victor requires continued haemodialysis twice weekly. His mother, Comfort Adesanya, said the family had spent over N20 million on his treatment and sold their land, house and other valuables to keep him alive. She appealed to individuals, corporate organisations and well-meaning Nigerians to help raise the N43 million required for the transplant, saying the family could no longer cope with the rising cost of treatment. Donations can be made to Victor Adekunle Olajide, UBA, Account Number: 2458216260 or call Victor on 09018866426. The post Unilorin student seeks N43m for kidney transplant appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Everything Is Breaking
items.description: You know things are bad when panic-buyers start emptying the shelves at Costco. As you might have noticed, everything is breaking. Over the past week, Outlook has gone down, U.S. air traffic control has gone down, banking systems have gone down, and the National Security Agency’s confidential-telephone system has gone down, and just today, Apple announced that some of its services are down. There is an air of something nefarious afoot. “If this is all a coincidence,” Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri said yesterday, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Others have traded apocalyptic theories: Are rogue AI agents taking over everything? Is this the End Times? The answers to these questions are, respectively: No, AI agents are not taking over, and isn’t it always the End Times? Let me explain. I believe strongly in Hanlon’s razor: Never attribute to malice what is easily explainable by stupidity or incompetence. So even on Friday, when the federal government halted all air travel in the United States just one day after a massive email outage, I was doubtful that these events were connected. But now mass outages and vulnerabilities to critical-infrastructure systems have surfaced day after day, sometimes multiple times a day. Even I have found it hard to shake the feeling that this is more than a coincidence. [ Read: What on earth is going on? ] There are three likely hypotheses to explain these events. The first explanation is benign: All of these breakages and failures are happening because we have old legacy systems that are running on outdated code. Crumbly old computer systems are crumbling. The second is more nefarious: foreign interference. This is not a crazy notion, especially given the crucial nature of the systems that have gone dark. (A special thought and prayer to the lucky ones who had to rebook a canceled flight on Friday night and couldn’t access their Outlook inbox.) The constant onslaught is also suspicious in light of recent events. U.S-China relations are at a low point after Jensen Huang was pushed out as CEO of Nvidia, in part for having an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence has reportedly identified as a Chinese spy. (China continues to deny that this is the case.) If not China, perhaps another foreign actor—possibly Iran. The third hypothesis is that third-party actors are using powerful AI tools to find a number of vulnerabilities and bugs in our digital infrastructure. But given that there reportedly have been no demands for ransom and no one bragging and claiming responsibility online, as is typical of hacking groups, this explanation seems unlikely. (Many ransomware attacks go unreported.) Hacks are very hard to pull off, Scott Shapiro, a cybersecurity expert at Yale Law School, told me. One hack after another across multiple sectors of critical infrastructure would be a feat so great that it seemingly could be pulled off only by nation-state actors—even in the age of AI. “What’s hard to understand is how these events could be stacked,” he said. “You would think that one is causing the other, but that does not seem to be the case.” I spoke with two federal officials, both of whom requested anonymity because of the classified nature of their job. Although not directly involved in the response to the outages, they did not see any reason to blame the incidents on foreign interference. That leaves one explanation: This is all (relatively) benign. Indeed, it turns out that a lot of stuff breaks all the time. Major outages on government sites , cloud services , and a number of low-profile systems have been going down over the past few months, all with mundane software issues brought on by new code slapped haphazardly onto old software. Moreover—and the government officials couldn’t emphasize this enough—high-level engineers who understand legacy code have left their job at the same time that there’s been an influx of people happy to throw anything they vibe code into the existing system. So when things break, as they are going to do, there aren’t people around who can fix them anymore. As for the timing with the Nvidia fallout, those I spoke with generally saw it as happenstance. Similarly, a number of people told me that the NSA communication system has been slowly failing over the past year and has had multiple (shorter) outages already. “No one is surprised about this inside the NSA,” an employee who works at the agency told me—an observation that echoes the agency’s own public statements . The biggest tell is in the solutions to these problems, none of which were particularly complicated or revealed any kind of virus, worm, or other type of hacking. Microsoft blamed the outage on a months-old bug. The Federal Aviation Administration cited problems stemming from a router update in Arkansas. Chase Bank attributed its brief outage to a software bug. “The solutions to these problems are banal, because the problem is banal,” one Defense Department official told me. “You run a patch. It’s fixed. That tells you right there what’s going on.” As tempting as it is to blame these outages on some Mission: Impossible –style foreign-bad-guy operation, there’s a lesson here: When you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras. But that can be a hard sell in the current moment of AI hype. It’s in vogue, among a certain set, to be an AI doomer and to worry about a grand catastrophic event that will render humanity either irrelevant or nonexistent. There is some truth to this: AI is responsible for the failures, but not because the singularity is here. Rather, most of the complex systems we run on are held together with duct tape. AI itself isn’t breaking those things; we’re using AI to break them faster. Most of our essential systems run on software that is old, out-of-date, and near-impossible to cohesively update. But now code changes are happening so quickly at the same time, and all sectors are losing the senior talent who are in the best position to stop these mistakes in the first place or fix them after they happen. In that sense, the outages are a preview of what AI disruption will really look like: not some swarm of Terminators, but everyday inconveniences that affect millions of lives and cost billions to fix.

items.title: Food security: Nigerian farmers risk wasting billions on fertilisers without soil testing, experts warn
items.description: By Adeola Badru & Cynthia Alo Nigeria’s quest for food security may continue to suffer setbacks unless farmers move away from indiscriminate fertiliser application and embrace soil testing and crop-specific nutrient management, agricultural experts have warned. The experts, who spoke at the 2026 South-West Nigeria Fertiliser and Soil Health Summit in Ibadan, Oyo State, cautioned that increasing fertiliser consumption without understanding the specific nutrient requirements of farmland could undermine agricultural productivity, weaken farmers’ incomes and worsen soil degradation. They argued that the country’s approach to fertiliser management must go beyond distributing inputs to farmers and focus on ensuring that the right fertiliser is applied to the right soil, for the right crop and at the appropriate time. The position formed a major highlight of the communiqué issued at the end of the summit, organised by the Institute of Agricultural Research and Training (IAR&T), Obafemi Awolowo University, Moor Plantation, Ibadan, on Tuesday. With the theme, “Fertilisers and Food Security in South-West Nigeria: The Journey So Far,” the summit brought together more than 150 scientists, farmers, policymakers, fertiliser manufacturers and distributors, agricultural extension professionals and development partners to examine the challenges confronting fertiliser utilisation and soil health in the region. The participants expressed concern that the continued reliance on blanket fertiliser recommendations failed to address significant differences in soil fertility, acidity, phosphorus fixation, nutrient depletion and other soil-related challenges across different agroecological zones. According to the communiqué, “The predominance of blanket fertiliser recommendations does not adequately address the variations in soil fertility, soil acidity, phosphorus fixation, nutrient depletion and other soil constraints across different agroecological zones in the region.” The experts maintained that fertiliser recommendations should increasingly be based on soil testing, crop requirements, prevailing agroecological conditions and economically viable nutrient management practices. They also identified high fertiliser prices, inadequate distribution networks, limited access to credit and inconsistent availability as major constraints preventing smallholder farmers from accessing and effectively utilising the agricultural input. The summit further warned that declining soil organic matter, nutrient imbalance, erosion and other forms of soil degradation continued to undermine fertiliser-use efficiency and agricultural productivity. To address the situation, it called on research institutions to strengthen soil fertility mapping and develop crop-, soil- and location-specific fertiliser recommendations for major crops cultivated across South-West Nigeria. It also urged governments and relevant agricultural institutions to facilitate affordable and accessible soil testing services to enable farmers to understand the condition of their farmland before applying fertilisers. The participants advocated integrated soil fertility management, involving the combination of mineral fertilisers with organic resources, crop residues, compost, animal manure and biological inputs, as a more sustainable approach to improving soil health and agricultural productivity. The summit also called for stronger collaboration between fertiliser manufacturers and research institutions to develop formulations capable of addressing specific soil deficiencies, including phosphorus fixation and shortages of secondary and micronutrients. On the impact of climate change, the experts noted that irregular rainfall patterns and increasing incidences of drought required farmers to adopt climate-smart fertiliser management strategies. They recommended that fertiliser application guidelines should take rainfall variability, planting dates, crop water requirements and appropriate application methods into consideration. The communiqué also raised concerns over the circulation of adulterated and substandard fertiliser products, calling on regulatory institutions to intensify inspections, product certification, market surveillance and enforcement of existing standards. It further recommended greater investment in digital soil maps, fertiliser recommendation platforms, mobile advisory services and precision nutrient management technologies to improve fertiliser distribution, application and monitoring. The summit stressed that sustainable fertiliser management should not be measured solely by increased crop yields but should also take account of environmental protection, farmers’ economic returns and the long-term preservation of soil health. It called for a coordinated monitoring framework to assess the impact of fertiliser interventions on crop productivity, farmers’ income, fertiliser-use efficiency and soil health. The summit acknowledged previous interventions by regional governments, research institutions and development partners to strengthen fertiliser and soil health systems but maintained that significant gaps remained in ensuring that fertilisers were affordable, accessible, appropriate, balanced and efficiently utilised. It warned that increased fertiliser use alone could not guarantee food security, insisting that sustainable agricultural production required sound soil health management, scientifically informed recommendations, effective extension services, quality assurance and supportive government policies. Earlier in his address, the chairman of the occasion and the Vice-Chancellor of Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, Prof. Simeon Bamire, who was represented by the Dean of the Faculty of Agriculture, Prof. A.O. Ajayi, emphasised the need to redirect attention from fertiliser distribution to fertiliser-use efficiency, describing it as a critical pathway to achieving food security. In his remarks, the Director of IAR&T, Prof. Gabriel Oluwatosin, noted that one of the key resolutions reached at the summit was the need to organise zonal fertiliser summits across the country, adding that without proper soil health management and fertilizer use, as the population is growing, farmers would not be able to secure their food food security. items.title: Conflict Escalation in Yemen - Situation Report #12 (Reporting period: 11 – 17 November 2026 | Issued: 17 November 2026)
items.description: Country: Yemen Sources: Health Cluster, World Health Organization Please refer to the attached file. Key Highlights Casualties continue, with Marib and Lahj carrying the burden. The HEOC count reached 12,779 (10,519 injured, 2,260 deaths) by 16 November, +1,024 in eight days. The daily average fell to ~128 from ~225, but reporting was incomplete (58–92% a day, none for 9–10 November), so the figures are a minimum. Between 11 and 15 November, Marib reported 266 casualties and 49 deaths and Lahj 234 casualties; Al-Dhale’e still has no funded WHO-supported trauma deployment. The front line is moving towards Aden. Front lines moved rapidly through Lahj and are approaching Aden, which hosts the main referral hospitals, the Health Emergency Operations Centre and the warehouse supplying the response. Further movement may change casualty flows and displacement, disrupt referral and supply routes, and require WHO and partners to adapt their operations. Measles–rubella campaign reached 92.3% of target. MoPHP results show 883,896 children aged 6–59 months vaccinated and 741,713 given vitamin A (77.5%). Al-Mahrah (61%) and Socotra (78%) fell short and 73,300 children were not reached. WHO-supported teams vaccinated 6,007 displaced children in five IDP camps in Aden and Lahj. Displacement continues to be at about 3,150 households a week. IOM DTM has recorded 347,321 people displaced since 1 August, including 18,780 in the past week, of whom 55% went to Lahj and 30% went to Taiz. Cholera is falling in the five most-affected governorates, but a complex outbreak is growing in Tarim. Suspected cases fell from 638 (W40) to 321 (W45). Tarim (Hadramout Al-Wadi) has reported 172 cases of acute diarrhea since W43, 78 RDT-positive and 22 culture-confirmed, with both suspected food and water. A diarrhea treatment center is being set up. Fuel and medical supplies are critically short in Taiz. Severe shortages of fuel, surgical supplies and anesthesia medicines are disrupting emergency services, including operating theatres and oxygen generation for intensive care units, and hospitals cannot sustain the continuous pressure. WHO delivered 19.6 MT of medicines and supplies to three facilities, and IRY and FMF plan to support two city hospitals. Shortages are also reported across the front line. Health facilities in areas under the control of the de facto authorities are reported to be short of medical and surgical supplies. Alternative delivery routes and access negotiations are needed to reach hospitals on both sides. The trauma referral pathway has critical gaps. Only four of the 35 planned trauma stabilization points are funded, none of them in Aden or in the part of Lahj towards which the front line is moving, and referral dispatch is unfunded. Burn cases are rising, yet hospitals can offer little beyond initial stabilization and wound dressing. Mental health and psychosocial support and rehabilitation remain the weakest links, leaving patients without continuity of care. Funding remains the binding constraint. All 32 WHO-supported trauma deployments are funded only until January 2027. WHO’s third CERF request is being consolidated at US$2.4 million, including sites, mobile teams and supplies proposed by UNICEF and IOM.

items.title: 655 tribunal registrars swear oath of secrecy ahead of 2027 election cases
items.description: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri With just 58 days to the general elections, the Court of Appeal on November 16 administered the oath of secrecy to 655 clerks and Deputy Chief Registrars selected to serve on the various election tribunals. The oath was administered under the supervision of the President of the Court of Appeal (PCA), Justice Monica Dongban-Mensem. It specifically invoked the provisions of Section 1(1) of the Official Secrets Act, which concerns the protection of official information. Under the Act, a person commits an offence if they transmit classified matter to a person to whom they are not authorised, on behalf of the Government, to transmit it. The Act also provides that a person is guilty of an offence if they obtain, reproduce, or retain classified matter which they are not authorised, on behalf of the Government, to obtain, reproduce, or retain, as the case may be. The officials were warned that the oath would remain binding even after their assignments at the tribunal ended, with the PCA vowing to hand over defaulters to security agencies for prosecution. “Is there anyone among you who did not read the oath form, or who signed it and now wants to withdraw from the assignment?” Justice Dongban-Mensem asked, as the weight of the oath dawned on the officials. “I am asking because you have just signed evidence against yourselves. Anyone we find doing what we have asked you not to do will be handed over to the Police for prosecution. “I am taking all the forms you signed to the secret registry of my office, and I will lock them in my safe. In case some of you are not aware, I began my tenure as President of this Court by handing some people over for prosecution, and they were duly prosecuted. “It is because people are not made to face the consequences of their actions that we have so many problems in this country. But at the Court of Appeal, we give you every opportunity to abide by your oath, and when you don’t, we prosecute. “Some of you may be approached and asked to give details of the tribunal members’ discussions. You will start eavesdropping to get information to pass on to them. “But when you eavesdrop, you can never get the full details. That is how, before you know it, false judgments start flying around. It often comes from the registry. “We are watching you, and many other people will be watching you too. Be very careful, be committed to the nation, and let’s get it right,” the PCA warned. Election Petition Tribunals are established to hear and determine petitions arising from the conduct of elections into political offices. Section 285(1) and (2) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, empowers the President of the Court of Appeal to constitute an Election Petition Tribunal in each State of the Federation and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja. Section 134(3)(a) and (b) of the Electoral Act, 2026 further provides that these Tribunals shall be constituted not later than 30 days before the election, and shall open their registries for business seven days before the election. The registry is a very important organ of an election petition tribunal, and its administrative duties include receiving petitions and other court processes for filing, serving court processes on parties in a timely manner, issuing hearing notices, preparing court proceedings and orders, keeping the tribunal’s documents in safe custody, and compiling records, among various other duties and responsibilities. The effectiveness, quality, efficiency, transparency and speed of the registry have a direct impact on the performance and justice delivery of the election tribunal. According to Section 285(5) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, a candidate aggrieved by the outcome of an election must file a petition at the registry of the appropriate tribunal or court within 21 days of the declaration of results by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). While the tribunal is statutorily mandated to deliver its judgment within 180 days from the date the petition was filed, any appeal arising from the tribunal’s or the Court of Appeal’s judgment must be filed and disposed of within 60 days from the date of the lower court’s decision. Addressing the 655 tribunal officials at the commencement of a two-day capacity-building workshop that followed their oath-taking session, Justice Dongban-Mensem noted that modern registry practices demand more than manual filing and routine administrative work. She said they demand a new mindset and the adoption of electronic filing and case management systems that allow for easy tracking and retrieval of cases. “They demand proper documentation, accurate and systematic archiving. They demand timely service of processes and effective scheduling that respects the strict timelines prescribed by law for election petitions. They demand confidentiality, integrity and professionalism.” She said the workshop, themed: “Modern Registry Practices for Effective Election Petition Tribunal Administration,” was designed as a platform to equip the participants with hands-on knowledge of the use of technology in case management, best practices in records keeping, and the ethical standards expected of tribunal staff. Emphasising that the integrity of the judiciary was on the line, the PCA cautioned the court’s registry staff against exploiting their election tribunal assignments for financial gain. “It is part of your obligation to discharge your duties with utmost good faith and not be carried away by little advances. “Your integrity and that of the Tribunal and its members are in the public searchlight. You must therefore ensure that you are not used as tools to derail the process. “Ensure that you live above board so that you do not bring the Judiciary into disrepute. Do not see it as an opportunity to enrich yourselves, but rather go there to build your name and your future, as it is said that a good name is better than silver and gold. “The Court will not hesitate to deal with anyone found wanting in this regard,” she added. For his part, the Chief Registrar of the Court of Appeal, Mr. Umar Bangari, said the tribunal officials must be conscious of the fact that “the spotlight of the entire nation will turn on the Judiciary” after the elections. He maintained that the success, efficiency, and credibility of every Tribunal rests heavily on the shoulders of the registrars and backroom staff. “You should be aware that you are the custodians of all the processes filed at the Tribunal, the managers of strict statutory timelines, and the primary administrative interface between parties on one hand, and the Bench on the other. “Accordingly, you are hereby placed on strict notice against engaging in any form of misconduct, including but not limited to collusion, conspiracy, or conniving with any party to manipulate court processes, alter records, or confer an unfair advantage upon one party to the detriment of another. “You must also avoid file tampering and leaking confidential internal communications, draft rulings, panel deliberations, or privileged case information to unauthorised persons, among so many other acts of misconduct. “We shall entertain zero tolerance towards any breach of neutrality or ethical standards. Any secretary or staff member found to be conniving with any party or counsel to subvert the course of justice will face severe consequences,” Bangari added. Noting that election adjudication is sui generis and strictly bound by constitutional and statutory timeframes, the Court of Appeal Registrar implored the participants to adhere strictly to timelines. “As we all know, a single administrative lapse, delayed endorsement, or misplaced process can occasion a damaging miscarriage of justice. You must treat every filing, service of processes, and transmission of records with utmost urgency and precision. “Avoid shady practices, such as giving litigants or counsel advance copies of processes. You should also avoid backdating processes in order to bring them within the prescribed time for filing. “Treat all Panel members of the Tribunal, as well as counsel and litigants, with courtesy, impartiality and professionalism. You are the first point of contact for litigants and counsel. “You manage the registries, receive and process filings, maintain accurate records, issue hearing notices, and ensure that the strict statutory timelines governing election petitions are never compromised,” he added. The Deputy Chief Registrar of the Court in charge of the election petition tribunals, Mrs. Maitumbi Altine, disclosed that a total of 223 of the participants have previously served in tribunals, while 432 of them are first-timers. She said it was the first time in the annals of the court that such training had been organised for staff members who will serve the various election tribunals. With the earlier inauguration of 375 judges who will serve on various tribunals across the country, the judiciary has clearly sent a loud message that it is ready for the aftermath of the 2027 general elections. The post 655 tribunal registrars swear oath of secrecy ahead of 2027 election cases appeared first on Vanguard News .

Review Summary: Significant local rains in the south, little rain in the centre and north. During 10–16 November, Bualle recorded 159.9 mm, Balcad 115.0 mm and Awdheegle 88.4 mm, while most stations in Bay, Hiraan and the centre recorded little or no rain. In the north, Las Dacawo recorded 50.0 mm and Elafweyn 31.5 mm. Satellite estimates (IMERG, 11–17 November) indicate 30–55 mm over Lower Juba and parts of Middle Juba and Gedo. By 16 November, 37 stations, 33 of them with a Deyr normal above 15 mm, had already received their full Deyr normal, including Baidoa (405.5 mm, 176% of the Deyr normal), Galkacyo (253.5 mm, 390%), Awdheegle (265.2 mm, 169%) and Bualle (240.9 mm, 148%), which passed its normal this week. Borama (16%), Burao (21%), Luuq (25%) and Mogadishu (27%) remain far below normal. River levels are rising slightly on the upper Shabelle and the Juba but remain well below flood-risk levels. Belet Weyne rose from 2.90 m on 15 November to 3.76 m today, 2.74 m below its moderate flood-risk level. Jowhar (2.90 m) and Bulo Burti (2.30 m) are falling, and Dollow (2.86 m) and Luuq (2.78 m) are rising slowly. Flood water in Jowhar district is receding. Satellite images show about 55 km² of flood water in Jowhar district, down from about 87 km² last week. Radio Ergo callers (5–11 November) reported flash floods that drowned livestock at Garadag in Sanaag and a death in stagnant flood water in Hirshabelle, while many callers in the south and centre welcomed the rains and said they had not seen the floods mentioned in the alerts.

items.title: AI, fake voter records raise new risks for 2027 elections
items.description: …Why media must not rush to publish election claims —Tech players By Juliet Umeh As Nigeria prepares for the 2027 general elections, voters may face a new kind of deception. The society is now rife with images, videos and audios that appear authentic but have been fabricated or altered. The concern has grown after the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, said it removed 1,609,553 records from the voters’ register following a technical assessment. The review examined suspected multiple registrations, unusual registration patterns, substituted photographs and irregularities linked to registration transactions. INEC also found cases in which some registration personnel deliberately bypassed established procedures, including provisions for exceptional circumstances involving persons with disabilities. The commission is investigating some flagged records. The findings have prompted questions about how the irregularities occurred and whether synthetic images or other AI-generated material could be used to undermine confidence in the electoral process. There is, however, no evidence in the material available that AI-generated images caused the irregularities in the register. Olaronke Alo of the BBC Disinformation Unit while speaking on Arise Television said its initial verification found that some of the images circulating online were present in the INEC register. She said: “What we did was to do the initial verification. We went into the INEC portal and began to trace some of the names and pictures being posted on social media. We found that these images were on the INEC register.” The unit also examined claims about inconsistent records, including one instance in which the same photograph appeared against different names. Alo said it found examples of apparently incomplete or unusual names and records alleged to belong to deceased people, including former President Muhammadu Buhari. She said the unit’s task was to verify claims circulating online, rather than assess whether INEC’s response was adequate. False claims can travel fast The risks extend beyond the voters’ register. AI tools can generate convincing images, videos and audio of people appearing to say things they never said. A fabricated statement attributed to a political figure could spread rapidly before voters have time to verify it. INEC has dismissed a social media poster and accompanying text claiming the commission had reaffirmed the leadership of the African Democratic Congress. The poster carried INEC’s logo and an image of National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna. With the matter before the courts, false claims styled as official announcements could mislead the public. Other risks include political messages tailored to specific groups of voters, fabricated result sheets, screenshots purporting to show updates from INEC’s results portal, or cloned voices announcing false outcomes. Such material could create confusion and deepen doubts about the credibility of the process. There is no evidence that these tactics have affected election results in Nigeria. But the possibility of manipulated content increases the work required of election officials, journalists and voters as the poll approaches. Alo urged voters to examine the details of material they encounter online, asking who posted it, why it was posted and whether credible sources have confirmed it. She cited a video appearing to show Burkina Faso leader Ibrahim Traoré addressing President Bola Tinubu in English. Viewers, she said, should consider whether the language matches what is known about the speaker and whether the video appeared through official channels. She said: “If a president is addressing another president, it is expected that the national broadcaster of that country is picking up those broadcasts.” Viewers can also look for inconsistencies in speech, mouth movements, skin tones and framing, she said. Reverse image searches may help establish whether a picture has appeared elsewhere and how it was originally used. People should also check official channels and note when platforms label content as AI-generated. No single clue proves a post is fake. But checking the source and seeking confirmation before sharing can slow the spread of misleading claims. Technology needs scrutiny At a panel discussion on science and technology during election season, speakers said the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System, BVAS, and INEC’s Result Viewing Portal, IReV, could improve transparency. They cautioned, however, that technology alone could not guarantee credible elections. Head of Research and Programmes at Kimpact Development Initiative, Oluwafemi John, said BVAS and IReV have different functions. “BVAS helps with verification and accreditation,” he said, explaining that the device checks voters through fingerprints or facial recognition. After ballots are counted, the presiding officer uses BVAS to transmit an image of the polling-unit result sheet, Form EC8A, to IReV. He noted: “IReV is not a collation point. We should not mix it up.” He said questions remained about the legal and evidential status of some election technology records, and urged the public to distinguish between uploading results for viewing and formally collating them at designated centres. A research analyst at the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development’s Digital Technology, AI and Information Disorder Analysis Centre, Sanusi Sanusi, said online access to polling-unit results had enabled independent scrutiny. He said: “Technology has really helped make election results transparent. If you know your polling unit, you can trace it on IReV and look at the result.” But he raised concerns about BVAS devices’ age and performance, citing reports of accreditation difficulties and compatibility problems. He also questioned how differences between electronically generated figures and figures on physical forms were reconciled. “If there is a disparity between the electronically generated figures and the physical figures, what is the reconciliation process?” he asked. “There is no guideline anywhere to explain that.” Sanusi said inconsistencies in voter figures and reports of missing ballots needed investigation and clear explanations. He cautioned that discrepancies should not automatically be called evidence of rigging without further verification. Verify before publishing For journalists, the challenge is not only interpreting results but also assessing suspicious digital material before it reaches the public. “Don’t run into publishing,” Sanusi said. “You need to develop your sense of doubt and figure out when something is worth investigating.” Tools that assess potentially AI-generated videos may offer clues, he said, but not definitive proof. “Always use multiple tools to verify.” The post AI, fake voter records raise new risks for 2027 elections appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Army seeks land for armoured corps training in Bauchi
items.description: …Commends Bala Mohammed for supporting military operations, infrastructure development By Christopher Ameh The Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, has appealed to the Bauchi State Government to allocate land for the establishment of a dedicated training facility for the Nigerian Army Armoured Corps in the state. Shaibu made the appeal during a courtesy visit to Governor Bala Mohammed at the Government House, Bauchi, where he commended the governor for supporting the Nigerian Army and promoting infrastructural development in the state. The Army Chief said the request had become necessary following the expansion of the Nigerian Army from eight to 12 divisions, a development that had increased the number of officers and soldiers requiring specialised training. He explained that Bauchi had remained a major training centre for armoured officers, noting that military personnel usually begin their professional careers in the state through the Young Officers’ Course and other specialised programmes. According to him, armoured officers spend more than 15 years of their military careers attending various courses in Bauchi before moving to other locations as they advance in rank. He said the proposed facility would provide a dedicated centre for the continuous training of officers and soldiers throughout the year. Shaibu disclosed that the Corps Commander of the Nigerian Army Armoured Corps would formally present the request to the governor, urging him to give it favourable consideration. “With this expansion, a lot of officers and soldiers have been coming into the Corps, and they will require this training consecutively throughout the year. Once that proposal comes, I crave your indulgence to please consider it,” he said. The Army Chief appreciated Mohammed for his administration’s support for the Armoured Corps, particularly the establishment of some military units in Alkaleri as part of efforts to expand the Army’s operational capacity. He also commended the governor’s infrastructural development efforts, describing the transformation of the Government House as remarkable. “Being an armoured officer myself and having started my career from here in Bauchi, I must acknowledge the massive infrastructural development taking place here. In fact, I did not recognise the Government House when I was coming,” he said. Shaibu further disclosed that he was in Bauchi to attend the grand finale of Exercise Mugunbugu, conducted in the Alkaleri general area. He described the exercise as the Nigerian Army’s major end-of-year training activity, designed to consolidate the various military exercises conducted throughout the year. The Army Chief also attended the maiden edition of the Nigerian Army Armoured Corps reunion and pulling-out ceremony, which attracted more than 100 retired senior officers. He said the reunion would provide an opportunity for retired officers to reflect on their contributions to the development of the Corps and share experiences that could strengthen the institution. Shaibu reiterated the appreciation of officers and soldiers of the Nigerian Army to the Bauchi State Government for its continued cooperation and support, expressing optimism that the partnership would further enhance military training and operational effectiveness. items.description: By Favour Ulebor, Abuja Ahead of the 2027 general elections, political analyst and lecturer at the International Institute of Journalists, Dr Austin Maho, has urged political parties to reject corrupt candidates, end the imposition of party leaders and introduce strict disciplinary measures to strengthen Nigeria’s democracy. Maho made the call on Wednesday in Abuja at the International Stakeholders Engagement Forum on Anti-Corruption, Party Building and Democratic Governance, organised by the Diplomatic Correspondents Association of Nigeria (DICAN). The forum had as its theme, “Nigeria’s 2027 Poll: Promoting Party Organisation, Discipline and Anti-Corruption Reforms: Lessons from Xi Jinping Thought.” Presenting a paper at the event, Maho called on political parties to introduce anti-corruption agreements for candidates, establish independent disciplinary committees and maintain credible membership registers to promote transparency and accountability. He warned that Nigerian political parties had increasingly become platforms for winning elections rather than institutions founded on ideology, discipline and national development. Maho also faulted the high cost of nomination forms, saying it was shutting out credible Nigerians from elective positions and encouraging money-driven politics. He said, “In China, the Party is an organization first, an election machine second. “In Nigeria, our parties are election machines first, and organizations almost never. “When we sell forms at that price, we are telling thieves to come and buy the ticket, because only thieves can afford it.” He urged Nigerian political parties to draw lessons from China’s approach to party organisation, discipline and anti-corruption while preserving the country’s multiparty democratic system. According to him, parties must strengthen their grassroots structures, ensure transparent congresses and sanction members found guilty of corruption, irrespective of their political influence. Also speaking, the Counsellor at the Chinese Embassy in Nigeria, Dong Hairong, said China remained committed to its anti-corruption campaign, disclosing that 8.1 million cases had been filed since 2012. She said 7.92 million officials had received disciplinary and administrative penalties, including more than 900 officials at vice-ministerial level and above. Dong explained that China’s anti-corruption drive was aimed at strengthening public trust, improving governance and ensuring accountability among government officials. She reaffirmed China’s willingness to share its governance experience with Nigeria and deepen cooperation between both countries. In his goodwill message, the Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Sola Enikanolaiye, said strong political parties and effective anti-corruption measures were essential to democratic development. Represented by the Assistant Director, Administration, in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Mahmud Aliyu, the minister said democracy should go beyond periodic elections to encompass transparency, accountability and respect for the rule of law. He urged political parties, civil society organisations and government institutions to strengthen democratic values and promote responsible leadership. Similarly, the Executive Chairman of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, Ola Olukoyede, called for greater public participation in the fight against corruption. Represented by the commission’s Head of Media and Publicity, Dele Oyewale, Olukoyede described corruption as a major challenge undermining Nigeria’s development, security and democratic institutions. He disclosed that the commission had secured 10,872 convictions and recovered N1.23 trillion within the 34 months of his leadership. He said, “The best diplomatic statement that we can make to the rest of the world is our commitment to the fight against corruption.” Earlier, DICAN Chairman, Idehai Frederick, said the forum was organised to stimulate discussions on strengthening political parties, tackling corruption and improving democratic governance ahead of the 2027 elections. He said Nigeria could draw lessons from China’s experience in party discipline and institutional development without abandoning its multiparty democratic system. Frederick urged stakeholders to develop practical recommendations for strengthening democratic institutions and promoting accountability in governance. items.title: 2027 countdown: Tinubu approves establishment of Kebbi inland dry port
items.description: …Tells Kebbi voters allow me complete 8 years ..North firmly represented in decision-making — Shettima By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA — President Bola Tinubu has appealed to Kebbi State voters to give him a second term to complete his eight-year tenure, promising that it would be their turn to produce the president thereafter. “This time, I am before you to seek your support for the second time to complete what I have started. It will be your turn next time,” Tinubu told supporters at the All Progressives Congress, APC, presidential campaign rally at Haliru Abdu Stadium, Birnin Kebbi, yesterday. The President said he returned to the state to thank the people for supporting him and other APC candidates in the 2023 elections. “You voted for me, you voted for Kaura Gwandu, you voted for our senators. Now I have come back to say thank you. May God bless you and answer your prayers,” he said. Seeking assurances of their support in 2027, Tinubu asked the crowd whether they had their Permanent Voter Cards, PVCs, and were ready to vote. “Are you ready to vote? Do you have your PVC? Raise your hand if you have your PVC. Are you going to come out and vote? Thank you very much. I can go home comfortably and sleep. I know you will come out to vote from top to bottom,” he said. Tinubu also announced approval of a long-awaited inland dry port for the state. “I understand your request on the inland dry port. That is a given. Kebbi needs it and it is approved,” he declared. He said requests by Governor Nasir Idris, including road projects and the reconstruction of a road damaged by flooding, were receiving attention. “All the requests of the governor are before me here. I have listed them carefully. We are working together,” he added. North at decision-making table Vice President Kashim Shettima, in his remarks, said the North was adequately represented in the Tinubu administration, citing key appointments in the security and defence architecture. He named the Minister of Defence, General Christopher Musa; Minister of State for Defence, Bello Matawalle; National Security Adviser, Nuhu Ribadu; and Chief of Naval Staff, Vice Admiral Idi Abbas. “The North sits comfortably at the table where decisions are made,” Shettima declared, adding that “a vote for His Excellency President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and for me as your Vice President is a vote for the preservation of the North.” He recalled Tinubu’s support for the North during the APC presidential primary, saying the President stood by the late former President Muhammadu Buhari’s preferred candidate. “He stood by the man who told delegates that he would never buy their votes with dollars. He made sure that the favourite of the North, the late General Muhammadu Buhari, became our party’s choice,” he said. Shettima said the North rewarded Tinubu in 2023 with 60.2 per cent of its votes and expressed confidence that the region would repeat the gesture in the 2027 election. On security, he said Tinubu had approved an increase of up to 80 per cent in the salaries of armed forces personnel. He also disclosed that the President had assigned him to chair a committee for the procurement of N200 billion worth of fertiliser for distribution to farmers during the dry season. Listing federal projects in Kebbi, Shettima cited the Sokoto-Badagry highway, with 258 kilometres passing through the state, describing it as the longest stretch in any state. Others include a 3.5-megawatt solar project in Ambursa and the upgrade of the Federal Medical Centre, Birnin Kebbi, to a teaching hospital. He said the College of Nursing and Midwifery, Ambursa, had been commissioned, while Kebbi State University, Aliero, received N693 million in student loan funding through the Nigerian Education Loan Fund, NELFUND. Shettima urged residents to vote for Tinubu on January 16 and return Governor Idris for a second term on February 6. APC leaders rally support Minister of Budget and Economic Planning and former Kebbi governor, Atiku Bagudu, said the APC was entering the 2027 election with greater unity than in 2023. “We are a more united Kebbi State here today, and we are facing the 2027 election more united than we did in 2023 under the able leadership of our governor,” he said. Bagudu credited Tinubu with bringing party leaders together, saying the President encouraged them to work together because the coming political task required “more hands rather than less”. The Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, urged opposition parties to learn from the large turnout, claiming that no previous administration had invested as much in Kebbi and the North as the Tinubu government. APC National Chairman, Professor Nentawe Yilwatda, said Tinubu deserved another term to consolidate his development projects across the country. The Speaker of the House of Representatives, Tajudeen Abbas, and Deputy Senate President, Barau Jibrin, also canvassed support for Tinubu and Idris. Former Governor Adamu Aliero praised Tinubu for approving the deployment of an armoured brigade to strengthen security in the state. Yobe State Governor, Mai Mala Buni, and former Kebbi governor, Usman Saidu Dakingari, also urged support for the President. Tinubu arrived at about 1.35pm, accompanied by Shettima, Yilwatda, Yari and serving and former governors. Thousands of supporters from the state’s 21 local government areas attended the rally, where northern pro-Tinubu singer, Adamu Dauda Kahutu, popularly known as Rarara, entertained the crowd. The rally followed an empowerment programme organised at the instance of the First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, which benefited at least 2,000 women in the state. items.title: Innovator develops machine to reduce drudgery in post-harvest cleaning of farm
items.description: By Cynthia Alo The use of manual methods to sort and wash agricultural produce, including tigernuts, ginger, potatoes and grains, may become less demanding with the development of a locally made machine designed to integrate sorting, washing and drying operations. The innovation, developed by a Kogi State-born physicist and innovator, Kabir Umar, is aimed at addressing the labour-intensive and often unhygienic methods used by smallholder farmers, cleaning artisans and agro-processors to prepare agricultural commodities for local consumption and processing. Umar said the absence of affordable integrated cleaning equipment had left many small-scale operators dependent on manual sorting and washing, while those seeking mechanised alternatives often had to acquire expensive imported specialised equipment. He identified tigernuts as one of the commodities particularly affected by the challenge, explaining that some cleaning artisans still use their legs to wash the nuts before sorting them by hand. According to him, similar challenges affect the handling of other agricultural commodities, including ginger, potatoes, millet, beans and hibiscus flowers, popularly known as zobo. Umar said the idea for the machine emerged in 2020 after he ventured into agro-processing and encountered difficulties with the cleaning and drying of raw agricultural materials, which he identified as an important first step in value addition. He subsequently developed a multipurpose post-harvest sorting and washing machine, with an additional drying capability, designed to provide an integrated cleaning solution for different agricultural commodities. The innovator said he had mainly used the machine to sort and wash tigernuts for further processing into tigernut flour, adding that demonstrations to tigernut cleaning artisans showed its potential to reduce manual labour and improve productivity. He, however, disclosed that the machine was still at an advanced prototype stage and had yet to be deployed sustainably to support farmers and other operators across the agricultural value chain. According to him, wider adoption of the machine could improve the quality of agricultural produce entering local markets, support value addition, create jobs and strengthen the export potential of Nigerian commodities by improving their post-harvest handling. On the challenges facing the development, Umar identified inadequate funding as a major constraint that had slowed the transition from prototype development to commercial production. He expressed optimism that intervention through the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure’s (NASENI) Innovate Naija Challenge would help accelerate the commercialisation process. items.title: Summit to examine financing, market access for farmers, agribusinesses
items.description: By Cynthia Alo Farm financing, market access and innovative solutions for farmers and agribusiness operators will take centre stage at the fifth edition of the Wealth Creation Summit scheduled for November 28, 2026, in Abuja. The summit, organised by Golden Harvest Acres Ventures, is expected to bring together more than 1,000 farmers, agribusiness owners, investors, entrepreneurs and young Nigerians to explore opportunities for improving agricultural productivity and building sustainable businesses. The event, themed, “Unlocking Opportunities for Wealth Creation, Innovation and Sustainable Agricultural Development,” will focus on connecting agricultural producers and entrepreneurs with financing opportunities, markets, investors and business development support. A major feature of the summit will be the launch of the Wealth Creation Network, an agribusiness and entrepreneurship cooperative designed to support farmers, women and young entrepreneurs through training, access to agricultural inputs, produce aggregation, market linkages and business development services. The network is also expected to provide members with opportunities for bulk produce sales, export linkages and investment-readiness training. Speaking ahead of the event, Convener of the summit and Founder of Golden Harvest Acres Ventures, Uzua Brainz, said the initiative was intended to provide participants with practical opportunities beyond conference discussions. “We do not want people to attend Wealth Creation Summit 5.0, listen to speeches and return home exactly as they came. We want them to leave with clarity, structure, connections and practical opportunities for wealth creation,” he said. items.title: Central African Republic BVD Readiness - DREF Operational Update (MDRCF034), 18 November 2026
items.description: Countries: Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of the Congo Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Please refer to the attached file. Description of the Event Date of event 17-05-2026 What happened, where and when? Between 15 and 18 May 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) declared an outbreak of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) caused by the Bundibugyo strain as a major public health emergency. This declaration was rapidly echoed by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC). At that time, the outbreak mainly affected three provinces in the DRC, namely Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu. As of 18 June 2026, a total of 33 health zones had reported confirmed cases, distributed as follows: 21 out of 36 health zones (58.3%) in Ituri; 11 out of 34 health zones (32.4%) in North Kivu; 1 health zone in South Kivu. These figures confirmed that Ituri Province remained the epicentre of the outbreak. According to WHO data available on 18 June 2026, the DRC had recorded 896 confirmed EVD cases, including 208 deaths and 78 recoveries. Cross-border transmission had also been reported in Uganda, with 19 confirmed cases, including two deaths and seven recoveries. Although the Central African Republic (CAR) had not reported any confirmed EVD cases at that time, the country remained at high risk of disease importation due to its proximity to the affected areas of the DRC. This outbreak, the seventeenth recorded in the DRC and the second associated with the Bundibugyo strain, had progressively expanded towards provinces located near the CAR border, notably Haut-Uélé. Available epidemiological information indicated a high likelihood of ongoing undetected transmission in this province, which serves as an important population movement corridor towards the border provinces of Bas-Uélé and South Ubangi. Furthermore, several public health alerts had been reported in areas close to the CAR border, including: The report of a death associated with a suspected viral haemorrhagic fever in Libenge Health Zone, South Ubangi Province, which hosts Central African refugees; A report dated 18 June 2026 from the Chief Medical Officer of Yakoma Health Zone regarding a suspected EVD case in a locality bordering Ouango-Gambo Health District in CAR. In this context, the combination of proximity to areas of probable transmission, intense cross-border population movements, repeated epidemiological alerts, and limited preparedness capacities fully justified the activation of a DREF preparedness operation. The operation aimed to anticipate and reduce the risk of EVD introduction and spread in CAR through proactive preparedness, community-based surveillance, and community engagement activities. However, the epidemiological situation evolved in a concerning manner, with the outbreak progressively spreading to provinces that share a direct border with CAR. In August 2026, Bas-Uélé Province, which borders CAR, reported its first confirmed EVD case in Buta Health Zone, becoming the sixth affected province in the DRC. The confirmed case was linked to travel from Haut-Uélé Province, highlighting the persistent risk associated with population movements between affected areas and border districts in CAR. As of 19 August 2026, the DRC had reported 5,208 confirmed cases and 2,476 deaths, compared to 896 cases and 208 deaths on 18 June 2026. In addition, 84 per cent of identified contacts were under follow-up. On the same date, another confirmed EVD case was reported in Viadana Health Zone, Bas-Uélé Province, in close proximity to the Haut-Mbomou, Mbomou, and Basse-Kotto health districts of the Central African Republic. The progression of the outbreak is particularly alarming. While three provinces and 33 health zones were affected as of 18 June 2026, the situation had expanded to six provinces and 55 affected health zones by 19 August 2026. This continued geographical expansion brought the outbreak significantly closer to the CAR border and substantially increased the risk of virus introduction into the country. Since the launch of the preparedness operation, sixty-four (64) suspected EVD cases have been reported and investigated in CAR. All laboratory test results returned negative for Ebola Virus Disease. By the end of October 2026, the regional situation had deteriorated further. Most DRC provinces bordering CAR were affected by EVD, including Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, South Ubangi, and North Ubangi. Geographical proximity, combined with the strong historical and family ties between communities living along the Ubangi River, facilitates significant formal and informal cross-border population movements. As of 25 October 2026, the epidemiological situation in the DRC reported: 10,060 cumulative cases; 4,887 deaths; 2,684 recoveries; 1,008 patients admitted to treatment centres; a case fatality rate of 48.6%; a contact tracing rate of 81.6%. These cases were distributed across eight provinces and 66 health zones or health districts. At the same time, the Central African Republic has progressively strengthened its preparedness capacity. The national preparedness level increased from 42 per cent at the beginning of the operation to 68 per cent during the latest assessment conducted at the end of August 2026. The 30-day acceleration plan validated in early October 2026 aims to raise this level to 95 per cent. As part of this acceleration plan, the Incident Management System has been decentralized to bring coordination closer to the highest-risk regions and their border health districts. Efforts are underway to make Ebola Treatment Centres fully operational in Obo, Bangassou, the Bimbo University Teaching Hospital, and PK24. Surveillance at points of entry has been reinforced, as have risk communication and community engagement activities, under the leadership of the Minister of Health. The Central African Red Cross (CRCA), which leads the Safe and Dignified Burials pillar, has trained fifteen teams of ten volunteers each to ensure adequate coverage of high-risk localities. Finally, on 22 and 23 October 2026, CAR and the DRC met in Bangui for a cross-border coordination meeting aimed at strengthening information sharing, exchanging experiences, and improving joint preparedness measures to prevent and control any potential spread of the outbreak in health districts on both sides of the border.

items.description: Este jueves 19 de noviembre es un día marcado en rojo para millones de inversores, el sector tecnológico de todo el mundo y la banca de Wall Street en bloque. El desembarco en el Nasdaq de Anthropic supone no solo la mayor salida a Bolsa de la historia, sino también una prueba de fuego para la fe de los mercados en la inteligencia artificial, puesta a prueba en un mes de fortísima volatilidad, dudas financieras y escándalos de alto nivel. items.title: Russian man accused of spying on US tech defence company that assists Ukraine
items.description: US investigators have arrested a Russian man who they say was recruited by Moscow to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm in California’s Silicon Valley that has links to Ukraine. Igor D’iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a spying operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco. He is also accused of stalking employees of the company and possessing falsified identity documents. The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia. US prosecutors say the company was targeted by Russia due to its assistance to Kyiv. “The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company’s assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia,” said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian. “We will not tolerate any efforts – by foreign governments or otherwise – to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations.” Prosecutors say that D’iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June. He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as “‘the Motherland’ and directed D’iu to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine”. On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software – tools he needed for his spy mission. He then went to a coffee shop located near the company’s offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there. His handlers also allegedly “instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity”. The suspect allegedly took photos of employees screens at a cafe near the office According to CBS News, the BBC’s US partner, the company in question is Palantir Technologies. Palantir did not reply to a BBC request for comment. D’iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences. On 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees’ cars on previous days. During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified – including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name “Hugo Landry Johns”. A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up two Russian passports, and a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees “family members’ names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses”, prosecutors say. He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty. The suspect was found with forged identification documents including a US passport He has been held in jail since 2 November. It is unclear whether he has hired a lawyer who can speak on his behalf. The arrest comes as espionage allegations roil the US tech industry, amid the news that Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic affair with a woman suspected of spying for China. Last month, a former OpenAI employee was charged with planting a listening device in a company office. The man was later accused of having “considerable support” from the Saudi government.

items.title: Festival « Clap ivoire » 2026 : Les lauréats togolais présentent leurs prix
items.description: Lomé, 18 nov. (ATOP) – Les lauréats togolais à la 26 e édition du festival « Clap ivoire » ont présenté leur prix le mercredi 18 novembre à Lomé lors d’une cérémonie présidée par le ministre du Tourisme, de la Culture et des Arts, Isaac Tchiakpé. L’édition 2026 de ce festival, placée sous le thème « cinéma et héritage : l’appropriation des récits africains par les jeunes cinéastes » a permis à deux réalisateurs togolais de remporter les premiers prix de leur catégorie. Ainsi, le réalisateur Biaou-Banna Ibrahima a remporté le prix du meilleur film fiction, d’une valeur de 1.500.000 FCFA pour son film « déconnecté ». Yélébo Amanou a quant à lui décroché le prix UEMOA du meilleur film d’intégration africaine, de 5.000.000 FCFA pour son film documentaire « murmures d’une mémoire ». « Clap ivoire » est un festival annuel de courts-métrages dédié aux jeunes réalisateurs des pays de l’Union économique et monétaire ouest africaine (UEMOA). Il vise à récompenser les meilleurs films de fiction et documentaires à travers une compétition en phases nationale et internationale. Le ministre Tchiakpé Le ministre Tchiakpé a félicité les deux lauréats pour avoir porté haut les couleurs nationales. Selon lui, « ces distinctions témoignent de la vitalité de notre création cinématographique et de notre capacité à faire rayonner nos imaginaires au-delà de nos frontières ». Le ministre a souligné qu’au-delà du succès que représentent ces prix, ils doivent aussi constituer des leviers de développement de l’industrie cinématographique. Il a inscrit la participation du Togo au FESPACO 2027, en qualité de pays d’honneur dans cette perspective. « Le Togo a des histoires à raconter, des talents à révéler et des images à faire découvrir au monde », a-t-il déclaré. Le directeur du Centre national du cinéma et des images animées, Koutom Essohanam Denis, a remercié les partenaires notamment l’Institut français et le Goethe Institut pour leur appui et accompagnement tout au long du processus de sélection et de formation des lauréats. ATOP/EAG/BA

items.title: 13è AG d’ARINWA: le ministre Ibrahima Sory 2 Tounkara appelle à traquer les avoirs criminels au-delà des frontières
items.description: À l'ouverture de la 13e Assemblée générale (AG) annuelle du Réseau inter-agences de recouvrement des avoirs pour l'Afrique de l'Ouest (ARINWA), ce mercredi 18 novembre 2026 à Conakry, le Garde des Sceaux, ministre de la Justice et des Droits de l'Homme, Ibrahima Sory 2 Tounkara, a lancé un appel au renforcement de la coopération régionale et internationale dans la lutte contre la criminalité économique et financière. Il a notamment insisté sur la nécessité de traquer les avoirs d'origine criminelle au-delà des frontières et de faire du recouvrement des biens confisqués un véritable instrument de justice, de bonne gouvernance et de développement. La Guinée entend faire de la coopération judiciaire un levier essentiel dans la lutte contre la criminalité économique et financière. En accueillant cette rencontre internationale, les autorités guinéennes entendent réaffirmer leur engagement à renforcer les mécanismes de coopération entre les États dans le domaine du recouvrement des avoirs saisis et confisqués. Dans son discours, le Ministre de la Justice a d'abord exprimé la satisfaction des autorités guinéennes de voir Conakry abriter ces importantes assises, tout en remerciant les responsables d'ARINWA pour cette initiative. Pour Ibrahima Sory 2 Tounkara, la tenue de cette Assemblée générale en Guinée traduit une volonté commune de consolider la coopération régionale et internationale face à des phénomènes criminels dont les conséquences dépassent largement les frontières nationales. « Le crime ne doit pas profiter au délinquant financier » Dans son intervention, le Garde des Sceaux a particulièrement insisté sur l'ampleur des menaces que représentent la corruption, le détournement de deniers publics, le blanchiment de capitaux, le financement du terrorisme et les trafics illicites pour les économies et les institutions des pays concernés. Face à cette réalité, il estime que la réponse judiciaire ne doit pas se limiter à la sanction des auteurs d'infractions. Elle doit également permettre d'identifier, de localiser, de saisir et de confisquer les avoirs provenant d'activités criminelles, dans le strict respect des lois en vigueur. « À cet égard, notre conviction est simple : le crime ne doit pas profiter au délinquant financier », a-t-il affirmé. Un principe qu'il considère comme fondamental dans la lutte contre la criminalité économique et financière. Le ministre a ainsi rappelé que la dimension transnationale de ces infractions impose une coopération internationale renforcée, afin que les frontières ne constituent plus des obstacles à l'identification et au recouvrement des avoirs d'origine criminelle. Dans cette perspective, il a mis en avant le rôle stratégique de l'ARINWA, notamment dans la facilitation des échanges de renseignements et le partage d'expériences entre les autorités compétentes. Il a également salué les efforts de la présidence du réseau, de son secrétariat permanent et de l'ensemble des points focaux pour le dynamisme de cette coopération régionale. L'AGRASC, un instrument essentiel du dispositif guinéen Abordant les efforts engagés par la Guinée dans ce domaine, Ibrahima Sory 2 Tounkara a inscrit l'action du département de la Justice dans la dynamique de renforcement de l'État de droit, de la bonne gouvernance et de la moralisation de la gestion publique. Sous la haute autorité du président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, et sous la conduite du Premier ministre, Amadou Oury Bah, le pays poursuit, selon lui, ses efforts pour consolider les mécanismes de lutte contre les infractions économiques et financières. Dans ce dispositif, le ministre a particulièrement souligné le rôle de l'Agence de gestion et de recouvrement des avoirs saisis et confisqués (AGRASC). Il a rappelé que cette institution occupe une place essentielle dans l'exécution des décisions de justice, la préservation de la valeur économique des biens placés sous main de justice ainsi que leur gestion rigoureuse et transparente. Une mission qui participe à l'efficacité de la réponse judiciaire et à la lutte contre l'enrichissement illicite. Les avoirs confisqués au service de l'intérêt général Au-delà des mécanismes de saisie et de confiscation, le ministre de la Justice a attiré l'attention des participants sur deux questions majeures inscrites à l'ordre du jour de cette 13e Assemblée générale : la coopération internationale en matière de recouvrement des avoirs et l'affectation des produits des avoirs confisqués. Pour lui, ces deux thématiques sont fondamentales pour améliorer l'efficacité des dispositifs existants et garantir que les ressources récupérées puissent contribuer à la réparation des préjudices et à la reconstruction des économies, conformément à l'intérêt général. Le Garde des Sceaux a notamment rappelé que les fonds détournés représentent autant de ressources soustraites aux secteurs essentiels du développement, notamment l'éducation, la santé, les infrastructures et le bien-être des populations. D'où son insistance sur la nécessité de donner une portée concrète au recouvrement des avoirs, au-delà de sa dimension judiciaire. « Le recouvrement des avoirs doit ainsi devenir un véritable instrument de justice, de bonne gouvernance et de développement », a-t-il déclaré. Dans cette logique, il a invité les États membres de l'ARINWA à renforcer leur collaboration et à privilégier des actions concrètes, coordonnées et mesurables. Cap sur une feuille de route ambitieuse pour 2027 Le ministre de la Justice a également exprimé la reconnaissance du gouvernement guinéen à l'endroit des partenaires techniques et financiers qui accompagnent le réseau, notamment l'Office des Nations unies contre la drogue et le crime (ONUDC), la coopération allemande à travers la GIZ, le projet SecFin Africa ainsi que l'ensemble des partenaires engagés dans le renforcement des capacités institutionnelles et l'amélioration de la coopération internationale. Pour Ibrahima Sory 2 Tounkara, l'ambition collective doit désormais être de bâtir un réseau ARINWA plus fort, plus solidaire, plus réactif et mieux outillé pour faire face aux défis de la criminalité financière. Il a ainsi souhaité que les trois jours de travaux débouchent sur des recommandations concrètes, mais surtout sur une feuille de route ambitieuse pour l'année 2027. La Guinée, a-t-il réaffirmé, reste engagée à poursuivre sa coopération avec l'ARINWA, ses États membres et l'ensemble de ses partenaires. Le Garde des Sceaux a par ailleurs livré un message qui résume sa vision de la coopération judiciaire face à la criminalité transnationale : « La lutte contre la criminalité financière ne sera véritablement efficace que lorsque les frontières cesseront de protéger les avoirs d'origine criminelle et que la coopération entre les États est plus que rapide que les mécanismes utilisés pour les dissimuler », a-t-il dit. C'est sur cette note de détermination qu'Ibrahima Sory 2 Tounkara a officiellement déclaré ouverts les travaux de la 13e Assemblée générale annuelle de l'ARINWA, donnant ainsi le coup d'envoi de trois jours d'échanges consacrés au renforcement de la coopération régionale et internationale dans la traque des avoirs criminels. items.title: Untraceable ASM gold could miss out on premium markets – Ken Ashigbey
items.description: The government’s 2027 Budget targets 100% local refining of artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) gold by 2028. But Dr Ken Ashigbey says local refining alone will not secure premium prices for the gold if it cannot be traced to responsible sources. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, the Ghana Chamber of Mines CEO said Ghana was already refining almost all the ASM gold it receives at the Gold Coast Refinery and the Royal Ghana Gold Refinery. He said the Gold Board had driven the process, although some gold was still being smuggled. Dr Ashigbey said ASM gold must be traced to its origin and shown to come from a responsibly mined and sourced place. Without that, he said, it would have to go to markets that do not pay a premium. “Then you don’t get premium from the gold that you produce,” he said. He called for continued work with large-scale mines and efforts to help ASM operators adopt responsible sourcing practices. Dr Ashigbey said the Ghana Chamber of Mines was working with the Bank of Ghana, the Gold Board, the Ministries of Lands and Natural Resources and Finance, and the Minerals Commission to supply feedstock from large-scale mines to the Royal Ghana Gold Refinery. He said the refinery was already processing responsibly sourced feedstock from large-scale mines as part of the process toward London Bullion Market Association (LBMA) certification. Dr Ashigbey said processing 30% of stock for about three years, followed by the remaining steps, would secure certification. Dr Ashigbey said LBMA certification is critical for the Bank of Ghana and other banks to hold gold in their reserves. He said improving responsible sourcing in the ASM sector would also significantly support Ghana’s gold beneficiation efforts.
