items.title: Rodrigue Guiguemdé, président de Digitales Solidaires : « Votre nom de domaine fait partie du patrimoine de votre entreprise »
items.description: La première édition du DNS & Brand Lab Ouagadougou, organisée le 29 octobre 2026, a mis en lumière un enjeu encore insuffisamment pris en compte par les entreprises burkinabè : la maîtrise de leur identité numérique. Propriété des noms de domaine, protection des marques, cybersécurité, promotion du « .bf » et souveraineté numérique ont nourri les échanges. Dans cet entretien accordé à Lefaso.net, Rodrigue Guiguemdé, président de Digitales Solidaires, dresse le bilan de cette initiative, revient sur les vulnérabilités des entreprises et présente les perspectives de déploiement du programme au Burkina Faso et dans la sous-région. Lefaso.net : Quel bilan général tirez-vous de cette première édition du DNS & Brand Lab Ouagadougou ? Rodrigue Guiguemdé : Le bilan dépasse nos attentes. Nous sommes partis d'une conviction : beaucoup d'entreprises ne savent pas réellement qui contrôle leur nom de domaine. Le 29 octobre, nous avons constaté que cette préoccupation intéressait de nombreux acteurs. Notre objectif n'était pas simplement d'expliquer le fonctionnement du système des noms de domaine (DNS). Nous voulions faire comprendre qu'un nom de domaine fait partie du patrimoine de l'entreprise, au même titre que sa marque ou sa clientèle. Le perdre peut entraîner une atteinte à sa réputation et, parfois, des pertes financières importantes. Pour Digitales Solidaires, ce Lab constitue la première traduction concrète de notre stratégie 2026-2030 consacrée à la confiance numérique et aux ressources de l'Internet. Nous voulions dépasser la sensibilisation ponctuelle pour proposer des outils et un accompagnement. Il s'agit de faire évoluer les mentalités : ne plus se contenter d'être présent sur Internet, mais apprendre à maîtriser son patrimoine numérique. Sur ce point, nous avons franchi une première étape. Le plus difficile reste à faire : transformer cette prise de conscience en pratiques durables. Combien de personnes ont participé à cette rencontre et quels étaient leurs profils ? Nous avons mobilisé une cinquantaine de participants en ligne, auxquels se sont ajoutées les personnes présentes au siège de l'Alliance burkinabè des domaines Internet (ABDI), qui accueillait la rencontre. Notre objectif initial était de réunir 35 à 40 personnes. La participation réelle pourrait être légèrement supérieure, puisque certaines personnes suivaient les échanges à plusieurs devant un même écran. Dix intervenants, issus de différentes organisations, ont animé les travaux. Le format hybride nous a permis de toucher des participants au-delà de Ouagadougou et de faire intervenir à distance des experts internationaux. Nous avons accueilli des chefs d'entreprise, des prestataires du web, des porteurs de projets, des étudiants, des représentants de l'ABDI et des membres des communautés Internet du Burkina Faso et du Bénin. Cette diversité était recherchée. Le nom de domaine n'est plus seulement une affaire de techniciens. Il concerne également le dirigeant qui protège sa marque, le commercial qui utilise une messagerie professionnelle ou encore le juriste chargé de la propriété intellectuelle. Quelles sont les principales préoccupations exprimées par les participants concernant les noms de domaine et la protection des marques ? Trois préoccupations reviennent régulièrement : qui contrôle réellement l'identité numérique de l'entreprise ? Comment la protéger ? Et que faire lorsqu'un problème survient ? Prenons un exemple fréquent. Une entreprise confie la création de son site Internet à un prestataire. Celui-ci enregistre le nom de domaine à son propre nom. Tant que les relations sont bonnes, personne ne s'en préoccupe. Mais en cas de différend, l'entreprise peut découvrir qu'elle ne maîtrise pas l'adresse de son propre site. Elle risque alors de perdre l'accès à son site, à sa messagerie professionnelle et à une partie de sa visibilité. Une autre difficulté tient à la confusion entre nom commercial, marque déposée et nom de domaine. Ces éléments sont complémentaires, mais ils relèvent de mécanismes de protection différents. Je rappelle souvent aux dirigeants que le coût d'enregistrement d'un nom de domaine est généralement faible au regard des conséquences que peut entraîner sa perte. Sa gestion doit donc relever d'une décision stratégique de l'entreprise et ne pas être considérée comme une simple dépense informatique. Quelle place le domaine national « .bf » peut-il occuper dans le développement de l'économie numérique burkinabè ? Le « .bf » représente notre identité sur Internet. Il constitue également une opportunité économique pour tout un écosystème national : le registre, les bureaux d'enregistrement, les hébergeurs, les développeurs et les entreprises utilisatrices. De nombreux noms intéressants sont encore disponibles. Les entreprises burkinabè ont donc intérêt à s'y positionner. Il faut aussi faire évoluer la perception du « .bf ». Certains pensent encore que cette extension est réservée aux administrations ou aux grandes entreprises. Or, elle peut également être utilisée par les startups, les PME et les associations. Cependant, le patriotisme ne suffira pas à convaincre les utilisateurs. Pour rendre le « .bf » attractif, il faut des procédures simples, des tarifs compétitifs, des services fiables et un bon niveau de sécurité. Le cadre institutionnel existe, avec l'ARCEP comme régulateur et l'ABDI comme gestionnaire du registre. Nous avons notamment suggéré la création d'un « Pack Lab .bf », qui pourrait proposer des conditions préférentielles la première année et un accompagnement à la configuration sécurisée du domaine. Au-delà du « .bf », l'Afrique doit aussi mieux se positionner dans l'industrie mondiale des noms de domaine, notamment dans les opportunités liées aux nouvelles extensions génériques de l'ICANN. Vous avez proposé un exercice pratique appelé « Domain & Brand Check ». Quels risques cet outil permet-il d'identifier ? Nous avons conçu cet outil pour aider les entreprises à détecter des vulnérabilités qui passent souvent inaperçues tant qu'aucun incident ne survient. Le diagnostic repose sur six vérifications essentielles : l'identité du titulaire du nom de domaine, la maîtrise des accès, la date d'expiration et le renouvellement, la protection du compte de gestion, la situation de la marque et la sécurité de la messagerie professionnelle. Ces vérifications peuvent révéler plusieurs faiblesses : un domaine enregistré au nom d'un ancien prestataire, un renouvellement non surveillé, un compte insuffisamment sécurisé ou encore une marque non déposée. Je dois reconnaître que l'atelier pratique a été plus court que prévu, en raison de l'intérêt suscité par les échanges. Nous comptons lui réserver davantage de temps lors des prochaines éditions. Les fiches recueillies sont en cours d'analyse. Il serait donc prématuré d'avancer un bilan chiffré des vulnérabilités identifiées. Notre ambition est de proposer aux PME un diagnostic simple de leur patrimoine numérique, adapté à leurs moyens. Quel niveau de connaissance les entreprises ont-elles des risques de cybersquatting, d'usurpation d'identité et des moyens de protection ? Il existe une différence entre connaître une menace et savoir s'en protéger. La plupart des acteurs ont entendu parler du piratage ou des arnaques en ligne. En revanche, les risques spécifiques liés à l'identité numérique restent moins bien compris. Une personne malveillante peut, par exemple, enregistrer un nom de domaine ressemblant à celui d'une entreprise, parfois avec une simple faute de frappe, pour tromper ses clients. Elle peut aussi créer un faux site ou utiliser une adresse électronique imitant celle d'un dirigeant. Dans ces situations, l'entreprise n'est pas la seule victime. Ses clients et ses partenaires peuvent également subir des préjudices. Pourtant, plusieurs mesures de prévention sont accessibles : activer l'authentification multifacteur, protéger le domaine contre les transferts non autorisés, sécuriser la messagerie et surveiller les noms de domaine susceptibles de créer une confusion. Il faut également connaître les mécanismes de recours. Pour les extensions génériques, il existe notamment la procédure UDRP. Pour le « .bf », un dispositif national de règlement des litiges est prévu, sans exclure les recours judiciaires. L'essentiel est de passer d'une logique de réaction à une culture de prévention. Quels retours avez-vous recueillis auprès des participants à l'issue de cette première édition ? Les nombreuses questions posées constituent déjà un indicateur de l'intérêt suscité par la rencontre. Les participants ont voulu savoir comment obtenir une nouvelle extension Internet, comment rejoindre AFRALO, comment régler un litige concernant un domaine « .bf » ou encore s'il existe des alternatives africaines aux grands fournisseurs internationaux de services DNS. Cette dernière préoccupation m'a particulièrement marqué. Elle montre que la question de la souveraineté numérique commence à intéresser les entrepreneurs eux-mêmes. La FED Numérique a également exprimé le souhait de voir le Lab devenir un rendez-vous régulier. Les participants attendent désormais des outils pratiques, une information fiable et des interlocuteurs capables de les orienter lorsqu'ils rencontrent des difficultés. Nous voulons inscrire cette démarche dans les programmes existants d'accompagnement des entreprises, plutôt que de créer une initiative isolée. Notre réussite devra être appréciée à travers les changements réellement observés dans les entreprises, et pas seulement à partir du nombre de personnes sensibilisées. Quel bilan tirez-vous de la collaboration entre les différents partenaires de cette première édition ? C'est l'un des acquis majeurs de cette rencontre. Nous avons réussi à réunir, dans un même cadre, des acteurs de la gestion des noms de domaine, de la gouvernance de l'Internet, de la société civile et du secteur privé. Chaque partenaire a apporté une expertise particulière. L'ICANN a présenté les enjeux internationaux du système des noms de domaine. AFRALO a mis en lumière la participation des utilisateurs africains à la gouvernance de l'Internet. L'ABDI a partagé son expérience de la gestion du « .bf » et des mécanismes de règlement des litiges. Internet Society Burkina Faso a contribué à la mobilisation de sa communauté, tandis que la FED Numérique a relayé les préoccupations du secteur privé. ECODEV International et l'expertise venue de l'Internet Society Bénin sur l'acceptation universelle ont enrichi les échanges, avec l'appui de Zepintel. Digitales Solidaires a assuré la conception et la coordination du Lab, en veillant à ce que les discussions restent proches des besoins des entreprises. Cette collaboration montre que la gouvernance de l'Internet doit être inclusive. Elle ne doit pas se limiter aux conférences internationales, mais produire des effets concrets pour les entreprises burkinabè. Quelles leçons retenez-vous de cette édition pilote et quelles améliorations envisagez-vous ? La première leçon est que les exemples concrets parlent davantage aux participants que les explications purement techniques. Lorsqu'on explique comment une entreprise peut perdre le contrôle de son nom de domaine, les enjeux deviennent immédiatement compréhensibles. Nous avons également constaté que les besoins diffèrent selon les profils. Une startup qui lance son premier service ne rencontre pas nécessairement les mêmes difficultés qu'une entreprise possédant plusieurs marques et noms de domaine. Il faudra donc adapter les prochaines éditions aux différents publics. Enfin, nous avons compris que la sensibilisation ne suffit pas. Nous devons mesurer les changements intervenus après la formation. Nous souhaitons accorder davantage de place aux exercices pratiques, proposer des diagnostics personnalisés, renforcer la participation des femmes et des jeunes et associer davantage de spécialistes de la propriété intellectuelle et de la cybersécurité. Nous aimerions aussi organiser des activités dans d'autres villes du Burkina Faso. Quelles sont les prochaines étapes du DNS & Brand Lab au Burkina Faso ? Notre priorité est de passer de la sensibilisation à l'accompagnement. Nous travaillons à la préparation d'un kit pédagogique comprenant notamment l'enregistrement de la rencontre, les présentations et des fiches pratiques sur le choix d'un nom de domaine « .bf », la sécurisation des accès et les démarches à entreprendre en cas de litige. Nous réfléchissons également, avec l'ABDI et les bureaux d'enregistrement, à un dispositif permettant d'orienter les participants qui auraient identifié des problèmes concernant leurs noms de domaine. Un suivi devra nous permettre de vérifier, dans les prochains mois, les mesures correctives effectivement mises en œuvre. Pour 2027, nous souhaitons faire du DNS & Brand Lab un rendez-vous annuel, avec des éditions thématiques destinées notamment aux banques, aux administrations, aux médias et aux acteurs du commerce électronique. D'autres pistes sont envisagées avec l'ABDI, comme la création d'un baromètre de santé des domaines « .bf » ou d'un label « Domaine de confiance .bf ». Nous prévoyons également d'intégrer ce module à Digitales Academy et de former des relais, avec un objectif d'au moins 40 % de femmes parmi les formateurs. Enfin, nous souhaitons proposer à nos partenaires un cadre de collaboration durable, reposant sur un comité de pilotage et une charte commune. Les indicateurs de réussite seront concrets : nombre de domaines correctement enregistrés au nom des entreprises, renouvellements sécurisés, messageries mieux protégées et marques effectivement déposées. Vous envisagez également des déclinaisons régionales, notamment le « DNS & Brand Lab Sahel » et le « DNS & Brand Lab OAPI ». Quelles ambitions portent ces projets ? Ces deux projets reposent sur une même conviction : le Burkina Faso et les pays du Sahel ne doivent pas se contenter d'utiliser l'Internet mondial. Ils doivent aussi participer à sa construction et à sa gouvernance. Le « DNS & Brand Lab Sahel » pourrait être organisé à Bamako, puis à Niamey, en associant les gestionnaires des extensions nationales « .bf », « .ml » et « .ne », les régulateurs, les bureaux d'enregistrement, les spécialistes de la propriété intellectuelle, les entreprises, les chercheurs et la société civile. Les échanges pourraient porter sur la sécurité du DNS, la gestion des extensions nationales, le règlement des litiges et la prise en compte des langues africaines sur Internet. Notre souhait serait d'aboutir à une feuille de route commune pour l'espace de l'Alliance des États du Sahel (AES). Le « DNS & Brand Lab OAPI » aurait une portée plus large. Les entreprises africaines développent leurs activités au-delà de leurs frontières, mais elles sont également exposées à des risques concernant leurs marques et leurs noms de domaine. L'Organisation africaine de la propriété intellectuelle (OAPI) permet déjà d'obtenir une protection des marques dans ses 17 États membres. Nous souhaitons rapprocher davantage cette démarche de la réservation et de la protection des noms de domaine. Avec des partenaires comme l'OAPI, l'Organisation mondiale de la propriété intellectuelle (OMPI) et l'ICANN, nous pourrions, par exemple, élaborer un guide commun à destination des entreprises. Il ne s'agit pas de créer de nouvelles institutions, mais de renforcer la coopération entre les structures existantes. Nous comptons également nous appuyer sur des réseaux régionaux, notamment le ROPTIC-UEMOA et Smart Africa, pour explorer les possibilités de mise en œuvre de ces projets. Le Burkina Faso peut jouer un rôle moteur en proposant des solutions utiles et en mobilisant les compétences disponibles. Pour conclure, quel message adressez-vous aux entrepreneurs, aux startups et aux PME burkinabè ? Je voudrais leur rappeler qu'un nom de domaine n'est pas une simple adresse Internet. Il porte l'identité, la réputation et une partie de la valeur de leur entreprise. On peut consacrer plusieurs années à construire une marque et à gagner la confiance de ses clients. Tout cela peut être fragilisé par une négligence dans la gestion d'un nom de domaine. Chaque dirigeant devrait donc se poser quelques questions essentielles : mon domaine est-il enregistré au nom de mon entreprise ? Qui détient les accès ? Ma marque est-elle protégée ? Que se passerait-il si je perdais ce domaine demain ? Nous parlons beaucoup de souveraineté numérique à travers les grandes infrastructures et les stratégies nationales. Mais elle se construit également à travers les décisions quotidiennes de milliers d'entrepreneurs. Pendant longtemps, nos efforts ont porté sur l'accès à Internet et la digitalisation. Ces étapes étaient indispensables, mais elles ne suffisent plus. Le défi n'est plus seulement de connecter et de digitaliser nos entreprises, mais de leur donner les moyens de maîtriser leur identité numérique, de sécuriser leurs actifs et de créer de la valeur. C'est toute l'ambition du DNS & Brand Lab : contribuer à l'émergence d'un Burkina Faso et d'une Afrique qui ne soient pas seulement connectés, mais qui maîtrisent et valorisent leur patrimoine numérique. Entretien réalisé par Lefaso.net

items.title: More Nigerian varsities make global list, few break into top 500
items.description: By Joseph Erunke Abuja—Nigeria has expanded its presence in the global university rankings, recording its highest-ever number of institutions in the Times Higher Education, THE, Interdisciplinary Science Rankings, even as the country struggles to push more universities into the world’s top 500. The latest 2027 ranking saw 27 Nigerian universities make the global list, a 50 per cent increase from the 18 institutions ranked in 2026. However, the country’s growing numerical presence has not translated into stronger representation among the world’s leading institutions. While the number of Nigerian universities participating in the exercise continued to rise, only two made it into the global top 300, against five in the previous editio Similarly, seven Nigerian institutions featured in the top 500, compared with eight in 2026. Amid the mixed performance, Covenant University, Ota, Ogun State, retained its position as Africa’s leading institution in interdisciplinary science, placing joint 49th globally to remain the continent’s only university among the world’s top 50 for the second consecutive year. The private university also maintained its lead over Egypt’s Cairo University, which placed joint 52nd globally, reinforcing Nigeria’s capacity to produce globally competitive institutions, despite persistent funding and research infrastructure challenges. Chairman of the Nigerian Tertiary Education Ranking Advisory Committee, NiTERAC, Professor Emeritus Peter Okebukola, who disclosed the results in a statement issued in Abuja yesterday, described the growing participation of Nigerian universities as encouraging but warned that the country must move beyond increasing its numbers to improving its actual performance. The 2027 ranking, released on November 18, assessed 1,058 universities across 102 countries and territories. It measured institutions’ capacity to fund, support and deliver research cutting across scientific disciplines. According to Okebukola, Nigeria’s performance represents a significant expansion from the 19 universities ranked in the maiden 2025 edition, while another seven institutions were accorded Reporter status after submitting data. This brings the total number of Nigerian universities participating in the 2027 exercise to 34, compared with 30 in 2026 and 27 in 2025. He said Nigeria had climbed from 16th to 11th position globally in terms of the number of ranked universities, retaining its second position in Africa behind Egypt, which has 37 institutions. Despite the progress, the ranking exposed the difficulty Nigerian universities face in translating increased participation into improved research competitiveness. Under the latest assessment, Covenant University emerged as Nigeria’s highest-ranked institution, followed by Landmark University, Omu-Aran, which occupied the 251–300 global band. Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, and the University of Ilorin were placed in the 351–400 band, while the University of Calabar, University of Lagos and University of Nigeria, Nsukka, occupied the 401–500 category. Ladoke Akintola University of Technology, Obafemi Awolowo University and the University of Benin completed Nigeria’s top 10, placing within the 501–600 band. Okebukola, former Executive Secretary of the National Universities Commission,NUC, particularly applauded Ahmadu Bello University and the University of Calabar for their remarkable improvement. ABU moved from the 601–800 band in 2026 to the 351–400 category in the latest ranking. , while the University of Calabar climbed from the 601–800 band to the 401–500 category. Eight Nigerian universities also made their debut in the global ranking. They are the Federal University of Technology, Minna; Michael Okpara University of Agriculture, Umudike; Joseph Sarwuan Tarka University, Makurdi; University of Jos; Rivers State University; Babcock University; Bells University of Technology; and Nile University of Nigeria. Osun State University equally returned to the ranking after a year’s absence. Of the 27 Nigerian universities ranked, 14 are federal institutions, seven state-owned, while six are privately-owned. Explaining the factors behind Nigeria’s relatively weak showing in the upper brackets, Okebukola identified inadequate funding for interdisciplinary science research, insufficient dedicated research facilities, weak administrative support and the absence of institutional policies encouraging collaboration across scientific disciplines as major constraints. He explained that the THE ranking uses 11 performance indicators grouped into three broad pillars: inputs, processes and outputs. While inputs account for 19 per cent of the assessment and processes 16 per cent, outputs carry the highest weight at 65 per cent. According to him, many Nigerian universities recorded poor scores in the inputs and processes categories, particularly in research funding and the institutional structures required to promote collaboration across disciplines. Okebukola commended the Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, for prioritising the global competitiveness of Nigerian tertiary institutions and establishing NiTERAC to coordinate efforts towards improving the international standing of the country’s universities. The post More Nigerian varsities make global list, few break into top 500 appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Recherche scientifique : Le Burkina Faso remporte le 11ᵉ Prix Vilho Väisälä de l’OMM grâce à une innovation pour la sécurité aérienne
items.description: Une équipe de trois chercheurs burkinabè a été distinguée par l’Organisation météorologique mondiale (OMM) pour ses travaux sur la surveillance automatisée de l’état des pistes d’atterrissage en temps de pluie. La récompense, remise le 7 octobre 2026 à Amsterdam, est assortie d'un prix de 10 000 dollars américains. Une reconnaissance internationale qui met en lumière le savoir-faire scientifique burkinabè. Le Burkina Faso vient de décrocher une nouvelle distinction sur la scène scientifique internationale. Une équipe de chercheurs burkinabè a remporté le 11ᵉ Prix du Professeur Dr Vilho Väisälä, décerné par l’Organisation météorologique mondiale (OMM), grâce à une innovation technologique destinée à améliorer la surveillance des pistes d’atterrissage et à renforcer la sécurité aérienne en période pluvieuse. La cérémonie officielle de remise du prix s'est tenue le 7 octobre 2026 à Amsterdam, aux Pays-Bas, en marge de la Conférence technique de l'OMM (TECO-2026) et du salon international Meteorological Technology World Expo 2026. La Directrice générale de l'Agence nationale de la météorologie du Burkina Faso, Dr Mariam Tidiga, a pris part à cet événement. À cette occasion, le Dr Dieudonné Sama, qui a présenté les travaux primés, a reçu au nom de son équipe le diplôme et la médaille récompensant cette recherche. La distinction est également accompagnée d'une enveloppe de 10 000 dollars américains. Une technologie pour surveiller les pistes en temps réel Intitulée « Global Reporting Format automation under rain: runway conditions monitoring in real time using Integrated Sensing and Communication technology », la recherche porte sur l'automatisation du Format mondial de comptes rendus de l'état de la piste (GRF) pendant les épisodes pluvieux. Les travaux sont le fruit d'une collaboration entre trois scientifiques burkinabè : le Dr Dieudonné Sama, chercheur principal, le professeur Doua Allain Gnabahou, directeur de thèse, et l'ingénieur Ali Ganamé. Leur innovation repose sur la technologie de détection et de communication intégrées, connue sous le sigle ISAC. Le dispositif utilise un lien radio installé le long de la piste d'atterrissage pour mesurer indirectement la quantité d'eau présente à sa surface. Concrètement, le système analyse l'atténuation du signal radio afin d'estimer, en temps réel, la hauteur du film d'eau sur la piste. Cette information permet de mieux apprécier les conditions de surface susceptibles d'influencer les opérations aériennes, particulièrement pendant les périodes de fortes pluies. La méthode a été expérimentée et calibrée sur le site de l'Aéroport international de Ouagadougou. Les résultats obtenus montrent une bonne correspondance entre les estimations du dispositif et les mesures de référence, avec un coefficient de détermination de 0,87. Une innovation qui pourrait réduire les contraintes des inspections L'un des principaux atouts de cette technologie réside dans sa capacité à fonctionner de manière automatique et continue. Contrairement aux inspections manuelles qui nécessitent le déplacement de véhicules sur les pistes, le dispositif proposé permettrait de suivre leur état sans interrompre les opérations aéroportuaires. La solution présente également des avantages en matière de coût et d'impact environnemental. Son caractère non intrusif pourrait faciliter son intégration dans les infrastructures aéroportuaires et améliorer la disponibilité des informations nécessaires à l'évaluation des conditions de piste. En période pluvieuse, où la présence d'eau sur les pistes constitue un paramètre important pour la sécurité des aéronefs, une surveillance fiable et régulière représente un enjeu majeur pour les professionnels de l'aviation civile. Le Burkina Faso parmi les pays africains distingués par l'OMM Au-delà de la performance technologique, cette récompense marque une reconnaissance importante pour la recherche scientifique burkinabè. Selon les informations communiquées, le Burkina Faso devient le deuxième pays africain et le premier d'Afrique subsaharienne à recevoir cette distinction de l'Organisation météorologique mondiale. Cette consécration met également en lumière le potentiel scientifique national, notamment celui de l'Université Norbert-Zongo de Koudougou, à laquelle les travaux sont associés. Pour les chercheurs, ce prix vient récompenser un effort collectif réalisé dans un contexte de moyens limités. Il constitue aussi une motivation supplémentaire pour poursuivre les recherches et développer des solutions technologiques adaptées aux besoins opérationnels du secteur aéronautique. La prochaine étape consiste désormais à finaliser le dispositif et à préparer son éventuel déploiement dans les aéroports. Avec cette distinction internationale, les chercheurs burkinabè démontrent que l'innovation scientifique peut également prendre naissance au niveau national et répondre à des problématiques concrètes. Une reconnaissance qui dépasse le cadre académique et ouvre des perspectives pour la sécurité aérienne, tout en donnant une visibilité supplémentaire aux compétences scientifiques du Burkina Faso. L’article Recherche scientifique : Le Burkina Faso remporte le 11ᵉ Prix Vilho Väisälä de l’OMM grâce à une innovation pour la sécurité aérienne est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: "Femmeblancherie" : le procès de la haine des femmes
items.description: Ce mercredi s’est ouvert le procès de sept membres du canal Telegram « Femmeblancherie » au tribunal judiciaire de Paris. Appels aux féminicides et aux viols, fichages racistes et homophobes, plusieurs dizaines d’abonnés sont accusés d’une trentaine de crimes et délits, dont « provocation publique à commettre un crime ». Un procès qui découle d’une idéologie très en vogue chez les jeunes, notamment sur les réseaux sociaux : le masculinisme.

items.title: Doctors risking heart disease through overwork, sleep deprivation – Experts
items.description: … Warn of burnout, stroke risks, seek healthier work environments By Chioma Obinna Health experts yesterday expressed concerns that Nigerian medical doctors are exposing themselves to increased risks of cardiovascular diseases, including heart attacks and strokes, through excessive workloads, sleep deprivation, chronic stress and failure to undergo regular medical checks. The experts, who spoke at the Annual General Meeting/Scientific Conference of the Medical and Dental Consultants’ Association of Nigeria (MDCAN), Federal Medical Centre (FMC), Ebute-Metta, Lagos tagged: “ Your Body, Your Responsibility: A Personal Guide to Cancer Risk Reduction for Physicians, lamented that physicians, despite their knowledge of healthy living, often neglect their own health while attending to patients. They called for a deliberate shift towards preventive healthcare among doctors, warning that professional dedication should not come at the expense of their lives. Speaking at the conference, Chief Consultant Cardiologist at the Lagos State University Teaching Hospital, LASUTH, Dr Folashade Daniel, said doctors must consciously balance their professional responsibilities with adequate rest, exercise, healthy eating and routine medical examinations. Daniel, who spoke on protecting the hearts of physicians, said: “I don’t think physicians can balance their work, healthy living, and their mobility. It has to be intentional.” She noted that doctors sometimes work for extended hours, leaving little time for personal health, but stressed that they must make deliberate efforts to recover and maintain healthy lifestyles. “First of all, know that your life is not just, your life doesn’t just entail your job. You are a person, you have a family, and you have responsibilities. Yes, to your patients, but also to your family, to yourself,” she said. According to her, doctors should make adequate rest, relaxation, healthy eating and physical activity essential parts of their routines, rather than treating them as optional activities. She advised physicians with a family history of cardiovascular disease to exercise extra caution and make annual health checks a priority. “Take your birthday, for example, your one anniversary, to do a check-up. And then look up all the results with a colleague. Don’t just be your own doctors. Let somebody look at what you have, the results you have done, and give you advice as need arises,” Daniel said. The cardiologist also urged government to strengthen policies that promote healthier food choices and safer working environments. She identified excessive salt, preservatives and trans fats in food, particularly from repeatedly used frying oil, as concerns requiring stronger regulation. Daniel further recommended accessible spaces for physical activity in workplaces, including walkways, trees and encouragement for workers to use stairs where appropriate. She said access to affordable medicines and wider coverage of the National Health Insurance Scheme was equally important in preventing and managing cardiovascular diseases. On the consequences of excessive working hours, she warned that sleep deprivation and prolonged shifts could expose doctors to additional health risks. Earlier, Chairman of MDCAN, FMC Ebute-Metta, Dr Lucky Okpetu, said the theme was chosen because physicians frequently advise patients to adopt healthy lifestyles but fail to practise the same advice themselves. “We found out that physicians hardly take care of them. They themselves don’t look after their hearts. They indulge in things they are not supposed to. They advise their patients to do the right thing. But they do not do what they tell the patients to do,” he said. Okpetu, a consultant haematologist, urged doctors to have personal physicians and undergo regular medical examinations. “The ideal thing to do is, as a physician, you must have your own physician. You have to see your physician regularly,” he said. He listed kidney function, blood sugar and other necessary medical tests among the routine checks doctors should undertake, adding that lifestyle choices remained critical to cardiovascular health. Speaking, the Medical Director and Chief Executive Officer of FMC Ebute-Metta, Dr Saheed Ogunme, also challenged physicians to make patients’ health and well-being their foremost consideration while strengthening collaboration between hospital management and consultants. He stressed that healthcare delivery was a collective responsibility and that no single professional could claim credit for successful patient outcomes. “If a patient comes to our hospital, has a successful surgery and goes home, it’s not the doctor or consultant that has done this alone. It’s the other people too, who participate in the care of that patient,” he said. Ogunme also urged doctors to pay attention to their own health, noting that physicians often have no personal doctors to consult when they become ill. The conference also examined the role of artificial intelligence in reducing workload and addressing manpower shortages in the health sector. Also, Professor of Medicine and Chairman, Medical Advisory Committee, FMC Ebute-Metta, Prof. Adebowale Adekoya, said AI could help reduce burnout by automating routine documentation and administrative tasks. He cited ambient scribe technology, which can listen to conversations between healthcare professionals and patients and convert them into clinical documentation. “AI can listen to conversation between the doctor, the nurse, and their patients. And then transcribe that using voice to text, using language models,” he said. However, Adekoya warned that doctors must verify AI-generated information before using it in patient care. “Although the responsibility of making sure that it’s accurate still lies with the caregiver of reading it before posting it,” he said. He also cautioned against applying AI tools developed using foreign population data indiscriminately to Nigerian patients, insisting that local data must inform medical technologies used in the country. “The responsibility is on us now to generate our own data,” he said. Chairman of the occasion, Prof. Oluwatoyin Ashiru, urged medical professionals to protect their physical and emotional well-being, warning that exhausted and distressed doctors could struggle to provide the quality of care expected of them. He challenged professional associations to protect the welfare of healthcare workers, strengthen institutional partnerships and ensure that professional disagreements did not undermine patient care. His message was clear: doctors must protect themselves while protecting others. The post Doctors risking heart disease through overwork, sleep deprivation – Experts appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Foursquare G.O. tasks graduands on integrity, national development
items.description: By Olayinka Latona The General Overseer of the Foursquare Gospel Church in Nigeria, Rev. Sam Aboyeji, has charged graduating students of LIFE Theological Seminary, Ikorodu, Lagos, to uphold integrity and sound biblical doctrine as they prepare to preach the Gospel and contribute to society. Aboyeji gave the charge at the institution’s 2026 graduation ceremony, where he urged the graduands to see their graduation not as an end but as a stepping stone to greater responsibilities in God’s service. Speaking on the theme of the ceremony, “Trailblazers,” and drawing from Titus 2:7-8, the cleric said the credibility of their future ministries would depend largely on the integrity of their personal lives. He said: “You have been equipped with knowledge and skills that must now find expression in faithful service to God and humanity. I charge you to distinguish yourselves as trailblazers whose lives exemplify the sound doctrine you have received.” Quoting Apostle Paul’s admonition to Titus, Aboyeji urged the graduates to be examples of good works, demonstrating integrity in doctrine, reverence, incorruptible speech and soundness of character. He warned against compromising biblical truths in the face of challenges, urging them to remain courageous, steadfast and diligent in their ministerial responsibilities. “Be courageous in breaking new ground, steadfast in the face of challenges, uncompromising in matters of biblical truth, and diligent in the discharge of your ministerial responsibilities,” he said. Reminding the graduands that service to God was a sacred responsibility requiring accountability to the Creator, the General Overseer urged them to remain worthy ambassadors of LIFE Theological Seminary and vessels of honour in their respective fields of assignment. Also speaking, the Chairman of the Governing Council of LIFE Theological Seminary, Rev. Joe Ameh, urged the graduating class to distinguish themselves as trailblazers and uncompromising ambassadors of Christ in a society increasingly challenged by moral decay and corruption. Ameh said the graduates were expected to demonstrate the values of Christianity and apply their theological training in addressing contemporary issues in a rapidly changing society. He said: “As trailblazers, those of you graduating today are expected to be ardent and passionate in distinguishing yourselves before a world characterised by normlessness and anomie. You are expected to be pathfinders in blazing the trail that should characterise the essence of being Christians with a fair measure of theological education in responding to contemporary issues in a fast-evolving setting.” The seminary council chairman also decried what he described as pervasive corrupt practices threatening the nation’s God-given assets and resources. He, however, urged the new ministers to remain steadfast and uphold Christian values despite pressures to compromise their standards. “Despite these pervasive corruptive tendencies, you are to be different in words and conduct and indeed be zealous to propagate sound Christian values irrespective of pressures to compromise our Christian standards,” he said. The post Foursquare G.O. tasks graduands on integrity, national development appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ukrainian FA to blame for failed drugs test – Mudryk
items.description: On-loan Tottenham winger Mykhailo Mudryk blames the Ukrainian national team’s administration for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban from football. The 25-year-old, on a season-long loan from Chelsea , was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium, which he believes entered his system while on international duty. Having initially faced a four-year ban from the Football Association (FA), his appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport was successful. He returned to football after admitting he breached anti-doping rules and agreeing to a suspension equal to the time he had already served. After appearing for Chelsea during a pre-season tour of Asia, Mudryk joined Tottenham on transfer deadline day to reunite with his former Shakhtar Donetsk manager Roberto de Zerbi. In a lengthy interview with the Ukrainian YouTube channel Guest of Gordon, Mudryk was asked who he blamed for missing the game. “The environment, the situation in the Ukrainian national team,” he replied. “It should never have existed. I probably haven’t said it publicly yet, but I’m saying it now. “I had never heard of a drug like meldonium. It is a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe. It could only have got into my body in Ukraine. There is no such drug in England.” He explained how he had only been in Ukraine to be with the national team and “it points to the fact it was in a national team camp”. Asked specifically whether he blamed the national team, Mudryk replied: “Yes, exactly.” He also said Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) president Andriy Shevchenko offered little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and claimed its handling of the matter delayed his return to football. Mudryk also said he spent millions of pounds on legal fees, coaching, pitch hire and private physiotherapy while being unable to access services at Chelsea . He added: “It was a bolt from the blue. I couldn’t believe it [the positive test] was true. “It was like falling off a skyscraper. In a dream you would hit the ground. In life, I just kept on falling. It hit me very hard, mentally.” Mudryk said he cried and drank alcohol after the initial suspension but never doubted that he would eventually return to top-level football. BBC Sport has contacted the UAF for comment. Last year, a UAF spokesperson told BBC Sport it was “in close contact with Mudryk’s lawyers” but had not been contacted by the FA about the case.

items.title: Mauritanie : adoption d’un décret en conseil des ministres fixant les conditions de promotion des médicaments
items.description: Le gouvernement mauritanien a approuvé ce mercredi un projet de décret fixant les conditions de promotion des médicaments et de contrôle de la publicité, ainsi que les procédures d'obtention des autorisations nécessaires à l'exercice des activités de promotion et d'information médicale. La loi n° 2025-042, promulguée le 26 novembre 2025, prévoit la publication de deux décrets visant à réglementer la promotion des médicaments, à fixer les conditions de fabrication, d’importation, de stockage, de distribution et de délivrance des produits cosmétiques et d’hygiène corporelle, ainsi qu’à en contrôler la qualité. Le projet de décret définit les règles relatives à la promotion des médicaments à usage humain destinés aux professionnels de santé et à la publicité destinée au grand public, ainsi que la réglementation des activités des délégués médicaux et les procédures d’autorisation préalable à l’exercice des activités de promotion et d’information pharmaceutique. L’adoption de ces textes s’inscrit dans le cadre de la révision et de la mise à jour de la loi n° 2010-022 relative à la pharmacie, dans le but de parachever le cadre réglementaire du secteur et de définir les règles juridiques régissant les différentes activités liées aux médicaments et aux produits cosmétiques. Cette démarche vise à renforcer le contrôle des produits commercialisés sur le marché, à garantir le respect des normes de qualité et de sécurité, ainsi qu’à réglementer les pratiques commerciales et promotionnelles liées au secteur pharmaceutique.

items.title: Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
items.description: When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history. In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia. But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide. “It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case,” says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. “It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state.” The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality. I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh. Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission . I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state. But the question posed at the UN’s top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide. Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled across the Myanmar border in 2017 as attacks on them grew The ICJ was established in 1945 to help settle disputes between states, not to try international crimes. However, it was chosen to address the attacks on Rohingyas in Myanmar because there were few other avenues of redress for the victims. Myanmar authorities have denied accusations of ethnic cleansing or genocide, saying they were only responding to terrorist actions by Rohingya militants with so-called military “clearance operations”. A UN report in 2018 , based on hundreds of interviews, said the army’s tactics were “grossly disproportionate to actual security threats”. It said top military figures in Myanmar must be investigated for genocide in Rakhine State and crimes against humanity in other areas. Myanmar rejected the report. As Myanmar was not a signatory to the International Criminal Court, it was not possible to file a case there against the officials accused of atrocities in Rakhine State. Instead in November 2019 The Gambia, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, filed a case at the ICJ, arguing that all states are bound by the Genocide Convention, so all have an interest in upholding it. It accused the state in Myanmar, not just the military, of genocide. This was a novelty in international law; a state not directly affected by an act, arguing that it had legal standing to make a complaint because it was indirectly affected by any violations of such an important convention. Myanmar objected to this argument, but the ICJ judges ruled that The Gambia was eligible to file the case. Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, was responsible for the military’s operations in 2017 The case drew even more attention when the Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who at the time headed the elected government in Myanmar, chose to lead the initial legal defence of her country at The Hague in person, for which she was widely criticised. She had very limited influence over the actions of the Myanmar military in Rakhine State, but her refusal to condemn them dismayed many of those who until then had admired her courage and adherence to democratic principles. Since she was deposed by a coup in 2021 and placed under arrest the defence has been led by a new team appointed by the military. Historically, proving that genocide has been committed has been very difficult. Judges apply a high bar to this. Typically, where there is no explicitly genocidal programme, like that of the Nazis, the judges require that the evidence presented at court must be such that the only reasonable inference from the actions of the defendants is that they had genocidal intent. When Bosnia-Herzegovina filed a genocide case against Serbia at the ICJ in 1993, it took the court 14 years to conclude that while incidents like the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica did amount to genocide, there was not sufficient proof that the state of Serbia had genocidal intent, though it was found to have failed to prevent genocide. Myanmar’s lawyers and Aung San Suu Kyi have argued something similar. Suu Kyi said that The Gambia’s team mischaracterised a complex conflict and military operation, and that while she accepted that war crimes may have been committed against the Rohingyas, that is not proof of genocidal intent. Aung San Suu Kyi’s refusal to condemn the Myanmar military’s actions in Rakhine State dismayed her admirers But Arsalan Suleman believes the weight of evidence his team gathered is enough to meet that high bar. “What we presented to the court was the long history of discrimination targeting the Rohingya, and how that history, and the policies connected with it, provide a background to understand the government’s language, rhetoric, propaganda, and policies that were part of the 2017 ‘clearance operations’,” Suleman said. “We discussed the 1982 citizenship law, and the tightening noose of discriminatory laws that restricted access to education, healthcare, livelihoods, and travel – all of which made life really impossible for the Rohingya and, we argued, was one of several indicators of genocidal intent.” What happens if the court does find in favour of The Gambia? Myanmar would then find itself tarnished by having committed “the crime of crimes”, as sitting on the same bench as Nazi Germany, the Rwandan Hutu militants and the Bosnian Serbs at Srebrenica. That might seem a setback for Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, who above all was responsible for the military’s operations in 2017, and who has been trying to improve his dismal international image in recent months. There is no right of appeal against an ICJ verdict. However, there is also no penalty that follows an ICJ verdict. The Burmese coup leader is focused mostly on rebuilding relations with neighbouring Asian countries, who are unlikely to pay too much attention to such a verdict, and much less on rebuilding relations with Western countries who do care. Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar mark the ninth anniversary of their exodus from Myanmar But for the huge Rohingya diaspora this verdict matters a great deal. “This is like formal recognition of our suffering,” says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of the Rakhine town of Buthidaung in 2017 and now lives in Canada. “For the Rohingya, this trial is a moment of acknowledgement of our suffering after years of denial. The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades, not just this year.” He and other Rohingya activists hope that a ruling in favour of The Gambia will prompt more co-ordinated action by other countries to find a resolution which allows them to go home to Rakhine State, in safety. More than a million are stuck in wretched camps in Bangladesh, barred from employment as international funding dries up. But the obstacles to realising this hope are formidable. Rakhine State has been ravaged by a conflict between the military and the insurgent Arakan Army, which now controls most of the territory. It is supported by the indigenous Rakhine population who are very hostile to the idea of the Rohingyas coming back. Many Rohingya villages have been completely destroyed. And international support for them has faded over the years. Even an unprecedented genocide verdict at the world’s highest court cannot change that reality.

items.title: Blindness: Eritrea, 10 others eliminate trachoma from Africa as Nigeria lags
items.description: By Sola Ogundipe Eritrea has become the 11th country in the World Health Organisation (WHO) African Region to eliminate trachoma as a public health problem, raising hopes of ending a neglected tropical disease (NTD) that continues to threaten the sight of millions of people across the continent. The achievement, validated by WHO, places Eritrea among 11 African countries that have successfully tackled the disease through sustained public health interventions, improved access to treatment, hygiene promotion and community mobilisation. Eritrea joins Algeria, Benin, Burundi, Eritrea, The Gambia, Ghana, Malawi, Mali, Mauritania, Senegal and Togo as the African countries that have received WHO validation as the number of countries that have achieved elimination globally stands at 34. Eritrea is also the 66th country globally and the 23rd in the WHO African Region to eliminate at least one neglected tropical disease. According to WHO, Eritrea achieved the milestone, following two decades of sustained interventions targeting the disease, particularly in remote rural communities where poor access to clean water, sanitation and healthcare had fuelled its spread. Eritrea’s success followed nationwide surveys conducted between 2006 and 2020, which helped identify affected communities and guide the rollout of interventions across the country. The government subsequently implemented WHO’s recommended SAFE strategy, a combination of surgery for advanced cases, antibiotics to clear infection, facial cleanliness to limit transmission and environmental improvements, particularly better access to water and sanitation. A notable feature of the campaign was its community-led sanitation approach, which delivered significant public health gains despite limited external funding. Health workers deployed digital tools for data collection and mapping to identify affected populations, track disease patterns and direct resources to hard-to-reach communities. In a congratulatory message, WHO Director-General, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said, “I congratulate the Government and people of Eritrea on this historic achievement. After two decades of determined effort, Eritrea has consigned trachoma as a public health problem to history. This is a victory for the communities most affected by this devastating disease, and a powerful example of what sustained national commitment can achieve.” On his part, WHO Regional Director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, said Eritrea’s achievement demonstrated the impact of political commitment, community participation and effective partnerships in tackling neglected tropical diseases. “I congratulate Eritrea on this historic public health milestone. It shows what is possible through sustained political commitment, community leadership and strong partnerships. Eritrea’s achievement brings us closer to a world free from the suffering caused by neglected tropical diseases and sends a strong message of hope to other African countries working towards trachoma elimination,” he stated. WHO Representative to Eritrea, Dr Mary Stephen, said: “This success belongs first and foremost to the people of Eritrea. The elimination of trachoma as a public health problem is the result of strong national leadership and ownership, and collaboration between communities, the Ministry of Health, the Fred Hollows Foundation, development partners and health workers across the country,” she said. While Eritrea has secured WHO validation, Nigeria is making significant progress towards eliminating trachoma, although the disease remains a public health challenge in some parts of the country. The Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare disclosed that 11 local government areas (LGAs) remained to achieve elimination status out of 134 previously identified endemic LGAs. The country has stopped mass drug administration (MDA) in 116 LGAs after they met the WHO elimination threshold, representing approximately 87 per cent progress towards eliminating the disease in affected areas. Director and Programme Manager of the National Trachoma Programme, Nicholas Olobio, said Nigeria had also performed more than 100,000 surgeries for trachomatous trichiasis, the advanced stage of the disease that can cause irreversible blindness. Nigeria’s progress has been hindered by the implementation of WHO’s SAFE strategy, supported by mass antibiotic distribution, eye surgeries, hygiene promotion and improved access to water and sanitation. Trachoma is among the 21 diseases and disease groups covered by WHO’s Neglected Tropical Diseases Roadmap 2021–2030, which seeks to accelerate prevention, control, elimination and eradication efforts, particularly among populations living in poverty and underserved communities. The disease is caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis and spreads through contact with eye and nasal discharge from infected people. Repeated infections can cause scarring of the inner eyelid, forcing the eyelashes to turn inward and scratch the eyeball. Without treatment, the condition can cause irreversible blindness. It disproportionately affects poor and underserved communities, particularly those with inadequate access to clean water, sanitation, hygiene facilities and essential healthcare. Despite significant global progress, the disease remains a public health challenge in parts of the world. Although Africa has recorded substantial progress, it remains the continent most affected by the disease. The global target for eliminating trachoma as a public health problem is part of WHO’s neglected tropical diseases road map for 2021 to 2030. items.description: By Islamiyyah Adekanbi Engr. Goodluck Idele’s decades of engineering work, including his involvement in building and delivering vessels for the Nigerian Navy and oil and gas companies, have earned him a Fellowship Award from the Nigeria Association of Technologists in Engineering, NATE. Idele was inducted as a Fellow at a ceremony held on Thursday, November 12, at the Dr. Obi Wali International Conference Centre, Port Harcourt, Rivers State. The award recognises his professional achievements and contributions to engineering. His work on vessels for clients in Nigeria and abroad reflects the technical expertise and commitment to quality that NATE cited in honouring him. NATE is an affiliate member of the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria, COREN. The ceremony brought together guests from academia, government, the engineering profession and the oil and gas industry. items.title: Eyesan seeks more opportunities for women in petroleum sector
items.description: By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja The Commission Chief Executive, Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC), Mrs. Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, has called for greater opportunities for women in the petroleum sector. Eyesan made the call on Wednesday while speaking on the topic, “Breaking Barriers,” at the 2026 Women in NNPC Limited (WIN) in Abuja, under the theme, “Powered by Her.” She asked women to also prioritise competence, resilience and continuous learning as critical tools for breaking barriers. A statement by the Commission said Eyesan urged women not to be discouraged by delayed promotions, stressing that professional growth requires patience, perseverance and commitment to excellence. Sharing her personal experience, Eyesan disclosed that she spent eight years in the same position without promotion but remained committed to her career. Eyesan also emphasised the importance of involving men in conversations about gender inclusion and women’s advancement, noting that some of the major milestones in her career were made possible by men who recognised her competence and provided opportunities. “I was appointed the first female Head of Strategy, not by a woman, but by a man who believed in my competence. I was also appointed as the first female EVP Upstream, NNPCL, by a man who believed in my competence, and today I stand as the first female CCE of NUPRC by Mr President, who is a man who believes that I will deliver,” she said. Acknowledging the gradual increase in opportunities for women in the industry, the NUPRC boss called for more deliberate efforts to achieve meaningful representation, advocating at least 25 per cent participation of women in leadership and decision-making positions. “Is it happening at the scale we want? Not quite, we need more. At least one in four. Not just because we want to make up the numbers but because we think we bring value to the table,” she said. The NUPRC boss also commended the Group Chief Executive Officer of NNPC Limited, Mr Bayo Ojulari, for the WIN initiative, describing it as a valuable platform for positioning young women for greater opportunities and leadership roles in the oil and gas industry. She noted that the Nigerian oil and gas industry was recording significant progress through collaboration between the regulator, NNPC Limited and other industry operators. items.title: Manchester won’t always be blue – Pochettino
items.description: Mauricio Pochettino says there is no time to waste as he sets out to restore Manchester United to being the city’s most successful club. The Argentine arrived to begin his new role as United manager on Wednesday after agreeing a two-and-a-half-year contract. The USA beat Haiti 2-0 in Cincinnati in his final game in charge on Tuesday, after which he spoke to TNT Sports., external Analyst DaMarcus Beasley, who spent the 2006-07 season on loan with Manchester City, joked that “Manchester is blue, it will always be blue”. Pochettino replied: “No way, you will see. Give me time, and that is going to change.” The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton boss flew directly to Manchester on a private jet after the game, landing at about 11:30 GMT before heading to the club’s Carrington training ground. Pochettino’s first game in charge is on Sunday, when United travel to face rivals Liverpool at Anfield (16:30 GMT). “I have plenty of energy. It’s a privilege to be head coach of Manchester United. And we are not wasting time. We need to be ready to compete on Sunday,” he said in his first interview to the club’s in-house media team. “Now it’s not time to think about rest, it’s not time to think about sleep. “It’s about being ready and to prepare everything to be sure that we are going to compete in the best condition at Anfield.” United are 18th in the Premier League having won just once this term, with Liverpool 14 places and 10 points above them. “We know that it is not a situation that deserves to be at a club like Manchester United and for the fanbase,” Pochettino added. “We’re excited because the new challenge is big, but it’s the adrenaline that you want to feel,” he said. “We are going to have a different job but we have the experience to deal with that. We need to add our common sense in the way that we are going to approach all the things.” Tuesday’s win ensured the US advanced to the Concacaf Nations League semi-finals and that Pochettino finished with a 62.16% win ratio from 37 games in charge. Mauricio Pochettino became head coach of the USA men’s national team in September 2024 The 54-year-old led the team to the 2025 Gold Cup final and the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup, when the US were co-hosts. “I am proud of what we achieved,” Pochettino said in a statement on Instagram., external “When we arrived, I wanted us to believe that we could compete with anyone. I hope today that belief is stronger, not only with the players but with everyone who supports this team. “This experience has re-energised me and given me so much, both in football and personally. “Leaving is tough at this moment, but sometimes in football an opportunity comes that is impossible to say no to. I have always believed in following my heart, even when it means leaving a place where I have been very happy. “I hope this team continues to grow and achieves all the success it deserves.”

items.title: Restoring Acheampong’s General rank would legitimise coup – Bomfeh
items.description: A senior lecturer at the University of Professional Studies, Accra (UPSA), Dr James Kwabena Bomfeh, has cautioned against efforts to reinstate the military rank of former Head of State General Ignatius Kutu Acheampong posthumously, arguing that it could give official recognition to a title he acquired after overthrowing an elected government. Dr Bomfeh, popularly known as Kabila, says the proposed restoration must be considered in the context of how Acheampong rose through the military hierarchy, insisting that the state should not confer legitimacy on ranks assumed following an unconstitutional seizure of power. According to Dr Bomfeh, Acheampong was a Major when he led the January 13, 1972 coup that toppled the government of the Second Republic under Prime Minister Kofi Abrefa Busia. He questioned why the Republic should be expected to restore a rank that, in his view, was not conferred through the country’s established military and constitutional processes. “Is it an attempt to go beyond the memorial lectures and say that the Republic must give him back his rank posthumously, which rank he only got by embarking on the coup d’état?” he asked. He argued that military officers who seize political power should not be allowed to use that authority to elevate their ranks and later expect the state to validate those titles. “Because at the time of the coup in 1972, January 13, Acheampong was not a General. At the time he did this, he was a Major. So they embark on coups d’état, take the power of the people, use or usurp the power of the Republic, and give themselves titles. Now, after they are gone, years later, you say that give them back those titles that the Republic never gave them or took away,” he said on Channel One on Wednesday, November 18, during a discussion sparked by calls for the late military ruler’s rank to be restored. Dr Bomfeh also disputed suggestions that Ghana’s historical treatment of Acheampong had been unduly harsh. “I sincerely think that Acheampong, properly speaking, has not been harshly dealt with in terms of the history of our country,” he said. He said any assessment of Acheampong’s time in office should separate the policies and projects associated with his administration from the circumstances under which he came to power. He cautioned against focusing on selected achievements of past military governments while overlooking the suspension of constitutional rule and the wider consequences of coups for democratic governance. His comments follow a renewed debate over Acheampong’s military status after business leader Sir Sam Jonah called for the former Head of State’s rank to be restored. Speaking at the second General Ignatius Kutu Acheampong Public Lecture Series in Accra on November 13, Sir Sam argued that Acheampong had been stripped of his rank by decree and executed on June 16, 1979, without being convicted by a court of law. He said restoring the rank would address what he considered an injustice and would not amount to endorsing Acheampong’s record in office. Dr Bomfeh, however, warned that the debate had implications beyond the military status of one former leader. He referred to Afrobarometer findings on attitudes towards democracy and military intervention, as well as developments in neighbouring Burkina Faso, to caution against public narratives that could make military takeovers appear acceptable alternatives to constitutional government. A September 2026 Afrobarometer report found that 65 per cent of Africans surveyed rejected military rule, although opposition to military intervention had weakened over the preceding decade. Dr Bomfeh maintained that Ghana must be careful not to create the impression that a coup can be retrospectively legitimised through state recognition, arguing that the country’s democratic history should be assessed with due regard to both the conduct of military regimes and the manner in which they assumed power.

items.title: UAC completes sale of 43% stake in DP World Logistics
items.description: By Peter Egwuatu UAC of Nigeria Plc has completed the sale of its 43 per cent equity interest in DP World Logistics Limited, formerly known as MDS Logistics Limited, to 22 Plus Invest Limited, a member of the Tropical General Investments (TGI) Group. Ayomipo Wey, Company Secretary and Group General Counsel of UACN, disclosed this in a statement sent to the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX) on Wednesday. The transaction, which was completed on November 18, 2026, followed approval by the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC). The company said the development followed its earlier announcement on September 24, 2026, of an agreement to sell its shareholding in DP World Logistics as part of its divestment plans. Commenting on the completion of the transaction, UAC Group Managing Director, Fola Aiyesimoju, expressed satisfaction with the successful conclusion of the divestment. He also appreciated the DP World team for its contributions to the UAC Group over the years, while wishing DP World and 22 Plus Invest a successful partnership and continued progress in their future business operations. Similarly, Vice Chairman of TGI Group, Farouk Gumel, welcomed the completion of the acquisition, expressing optimism about the partnership with DP World. Gumel said the partnership would focus on advancing a shared vision for Africa’s trade and logistics sector, particularly by strengthening supply chains, improving regional connectivity and creating long-term value for customers and economies across the continent. He added that the acquisition marked a new phase for DP World Logistics under its new ownership and was expected to support efforts to strengthen logistics operations and trade connectivity across Africa. items.title: LBMA certification could unlock higher gold export values for Ghana – Manteaw
items.description: Ghana could earn more from gold exports and access mainstream markets if it backs its local refining drive with LBMA certification, Dr Steven Manteaw said. The Co-chair of the Ghana Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (GHEITI) says certification would help the country secure greater economic benefits from refining gold locally. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, he linked those potential gains to the government’s target of refining all artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) gold locally by 2028. The target, set in the 2027 budget, aims to move the country toward 100% local refining of ASM gold. Dr Manteaw said undertaking that refining under LBMA certification would help the economy. It would enable Ghana to reach mainstream markets and “get higher values for our gold exports”. His assessment places certification alongside refinery expansion as a key consideration in delivering the government’s ambition. When asked by host Evans Mensah whether the 2028 target was achievable, Dr Manteaw expressed confidence that Ghana could deliver. “Well, it is doable, and we need to expand the refinery infrastructure,” he said. But processing capacity alone would not be enough. He also stressed the need to reduce smuggling and secure sufficient gold to supply the refineries. Ghana must “reduce smuggling and get the feedstock”, he said. Dr Manteaw argued that adding value to gold was less difficult than doing so for some other minerals. “It is not like the industrial minerals, bauxites, manganese, and the rest; those are a bit difficult.” While backing the objective, he called for the government to show how it intends to achieve it. “Want to see the plan that the government has for achieving that laudable objective.”

items.title: Acheampong inherited housing, agriculture plans – Bomfeh
items.description: A Senior Lecturer at the University of Professional Studies, Accra (UPSA), Dr James Kwabena Bomfeh has challenged the attribution of some major development projects to the regime of former Head of State General Ignatius Kutu Acheampong, arguing that the administration built on initiatives conceived by earlier governments. He says the Dansoman housing estate and other residential developments often cited as achievements of the Acheampong era were part of a housing policy direction established long before the military ruler seized power in January 1972. Dr Bomfeh made the observation on Channel One TV on Wednesday, November 18, as debate over Acheampong’s legacy gathered momentum. He cited developments at Tema Township, North Kaneshie and the Kwame Nkrumah Estates as evidence that large-scale estate housing was already on Ghana’s development agenda under the First Republic. “Was it the first estate development in Ghana? No. There was a blueprint. Tema Township, North Kaneshie, Kwame Nkrumah Estates. They were there. Estate development was part of the development programme of the First Republic,” he said. Dr Bomfeh argued that the history of projects completed or advanced during Acheampong’s tenure should not be told without examining the policies and plans inherited by his administration. He extended the argument to the former regime’s flagship Operation Feed Yourself programme, suggesting that its agricultural policy foundations also had antecedents in earlier governments. For him, crediting a military administration with development projects without tracing their origins risks presenting an incomplete account of Ghana’s political and economic history. He said the assessment of Acheampong’s record should go beyond the infrastructure and agricultural initiatives associated with his rule to examine the broader consequences of the coup that brought him to power. “If we want to look at the positives that came from Acheampong’s unconstitutional overthrow of the constitutional government of the Republic of Ghana in the Second Republic, we must as well discuss the cost to the country. What did it cost us and for how long?” he asked. Dr Bomfeh maintained that Ghana’s repeated military interventions had disrupted democratic governance and weakened the development of institutions, warning against using projects undertaken by military regimes to justify the overthrow of elected governments. His comments add another dimension to the ongoing debate over Acheampong’s place in Ghana’s history, following renewed calls for the former Head of State’s military rank to be restored posthumously. The debate has drawn attention to how the country should assess the legacies of past military rulers, including the distinction between policies and projects undertaken during their administrations and the constitutional circumstances under which they assumed power.

items.title: Burkina Faso : Les populations du Nakambé s’approprient la campagne de communication sanitaire en langues nationales
items.description: La campagne du « Mois de la communication sanitaire en langues nationales » bat son plein dans la région du Nakambé. Après Ziniaré et Fada N’Gourma, les journalistes participant à la caravane de presse du ministère de la Santé ont fait escale à Tenkodogo, ce 18 novembre 2026. Cette troisième étape a permis de découvrir les réalisations sanitaires enregistrées au cours des quatre dernières années sous le régime du Mouvement patriotique pour la sauvegarde de la patrie (MPSR 2), mais aussi d’aller à la rencontre des acteurs de terrain et des auditeurs. Sur le plan des infrastructures, la région du Nakambé a bénéficié de la construction et de la mise en service de nombreuses structures, parmi lesquelles 45 centres de santé et de promotion sociale (CSPS) et de nouveaux centres médicaux. À cela s'ajoutent la mise en place de projets de dialyse et de services de réanimation. Ces structures ont également été dotées d'équipements de pointe. Il s’agit de tables d'opération, d'autoclaves, de groupes électrogènes, de cliniques mobiles et de réfrigérateurs à vaccins. Elles ont en outre reçu un important matériel roulant, avec 18 ambulances et 7 véhicules de supervision. Le volet humain n'est pas en reste, comme l'a souligné le Dr Lendé Tougri, directeur régional de la Santé du Nakambé. Le volet humain n'est pas en reste, comme l'a souligné le Dr Lendé Tougri, directeur régional de la Santé du Nakambé -©Faso7 « La région a bénéficié de beaucoup de ressources humaines depuis les quatre années du MPSR2. Rien que pour 2026, nous avons eu environ 200 agents de santé, tous profils confondus : spécialistes, infirmiers, sages-femmes et médecins généralistes, afin d'augmenter l'offre de soins dans la région du Nakambé » , a-t-il expliqué. Pour porter les messages de santé publique au plus près des citoyens, 14 stations de radio accompagnent le ministère dans cette campagne. Les programmes sont ainsi diffusés en mooré, bissa, yaana, fulfuldé et gourmantchéma. La santé maternelle et infantile Cette étape a aussi permis aux journalistes de suivre une émission en direct et de recueillir l'avis des auditeurs. Céline Koala, auditrice de la radio Liberté de parler et de communiquer (LPT), se réjouit de la diffusion d'émissions de santé en langues nationales. Selon elle, cela permet à la grande majorité des populations de mieux comprendre les enjeux de la santé maternelle et infantile. « Animer l'émission en langue est une bonne chose, car cela permet à nos mamans, à nous-mêmes et à tout le monde de bien comprendre et de prendre au sérieux la santé de la mère et de l'enfant », a-t-elle déclaré. Kobiané Adama, infirmier chef de poste au CSPS urbain 2 de Tenkodogo, a souligné que les structures sanitaires s'adaptent aux besoins des populations en menant de longue date des actions de sensibilisation dans les langues locales. Pour lui, le mois de la communication vient renforcer les initiatives existantes, à travers des sorties de stratégie avancée dans les villages et la mise en place de sites de sensibilisation au sein de la formation sanitaire. « Les doléances des populations sont satisfaites. Elles souhaitent que ces initiatives soient pérennes et étendues partout, car plus on parle d'une situation dans la langue nationale, mieux la personne comprend, contrairement aux mots en français », a-t-il indiqué.
