items.title: ‘No Take, Only Throw’ Politics
items.description: This month, fed-up, stressed-out Americans headed to the ballot box and tacked hard to the left, supporting the party that is promising to restore billions of dollars in federal spending and billions of dollars in federal tax revenue. Democrats won in blue states. They won in purple states, such as Georgia, Michigan, Maine, and North Carolina. They flipped seats in Trump-hat-red Nebraska, Indiana, Kentucky, Texas, Iowa, and Montana. Voters in South Carolina sent a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since 1998; in Mississippi, since 1982. At the same time, fed-up, stressed-out Americans headed to the ballot box and curved to the right, supporting a bevy of measures to restrain government spending . Some revenue-raising initiatives won; Coloradans created a graduated state income tax, for instance. But in Florida, voters gutted the property-tax system. In Louisiana, they sheltered seniors from taxation. In Arizona, they limited levies on groceries and banned them on vehicle-miles traveled. In progressive California, they turned down a onetime wealth tax on billionaires and made it harder for the state to impose one in the future. The midterm landslide was another instance of the electorate rejecting incumbents and revolting against the establishment. It was another example of American voters raging against the country’s brutal cost-of-living crisis. It was also a triumph of what I have come to think of as “no take, only throw” politics, a reference to an old Tumblr meme, itself a reference to a common experience among dog people: Fido demands that his human servant throw the ball, but won’t drop it. That’s politics today, more or less. Voters want big-government budgets and small-government taxes. Politicians act like they can give it to them. cupcakelogic / Tumblr But you can’t throw without taking unless you have a pocket full of tennis balls, which the United States Treasury, at the moment, does not. Americans can turn the tax code into Swiss cheese and keep levies on middle-class and upper-middle-class families low. They can spend trillions on initiatives to bolster the spending power of working households. They cannot do both of those things while keeping politically and societally destabilizing inflation in check. Inflation hasn’t been in check since the arrival of the coronavirus pandemic. Prices are increasing nearly twice as fast as the Federal Reserve wants them to, and the costs of many essential goods and services are spiking even faster. Gas prices shot up nearly 60 percent from January to May. Employer-sponsored insurance premiums jumped 5 percent this year and are expected to increase another 8 percent to 11 percent next year. (The premiums on marketplace plans will rise as much as 13 percent come 2027.) The price of electricity has risen 11 percent year over year in Idaho, 14 percent in Maine, and 23 percent in Hawaii. The price of home insurance is up 9 percent around the country. Even coffee costs 41 percent more than it did two years ago, if you buy ground beans to brew at home. These isolated bumps add up, compound, and bleed families dry. If prices had increased at the central bank’s target rate since Donald Trump was reelected, the typical middle-class family would have $1,800 more in its bank account than it does right now—cash to spend on Christmas presents or invest in a retirement fund. If inflation had been subdued since Joe Biden’s election, that same family would have saved more than $36,000 on everyday expenses. That’s enough to buy a used car. It’s a big chunk of a down payment on a typical apartment. The post-COVID bout of inflation is not in and of itself responsible for the country’s cost-of-living crisis, which has been decades in the making. Land-use restrictions have throttled the housing supply, pushing up prices in dense cities and remote towns. A surfeit of subsidies, lack of cost controls, and consolidation in the health-care market has spurred insurers to jack up the price of coverage. Still, not only has Washington failed to fix the housing shortage and rationalize the health-care system; it has stoked price increases across the whole economy. This year, it is spending $2 trillion more than it is receiving in revenue, a budget deficit equivalent to 6.2 percent of GDP. That’s almost as big a stimulus as the government was running in 2012, during the miserable jobless recovery from the Great Recession. Back then, the country desperately needed the deficit spending: The unemployment rate was four percentage points higher and the GDP growth rate markedly lower. Now Washington’s largesse is pumping up prices, forcing up interest rates, and making the rich richer. Indeed, Trump’s signature tax bill slashed federal tax revenue by $460 billion this year alone, with much of the relief going to wealthy households and wealthy corporations. (I should be fair: He did soak up some of the red ink by defunding HIV-prevention programs and taking food stamps away from kids.) On top of that, Trump has engaged in a foolish trade war, driving up the cost of imported goods. He has engaged in a foolish war on immigration, shrinking the labor pool and increasing the cost of child care and construction. He has engaged in a foolish actual war, pushing up the cost of oil and gas. He has also promoted the AI build-out, which has pumped up borrowing costs and utility bills. Democrats have regained power promising to undo Trump’s policies, in particular his cuts to Medicaid, SNAP, and health-insurance subsidies. It’s a priority for affordability reasons and moral reasons as well. The SNAP cuts are already stoking widespread food insecurity in Arizona, Florida, Georgia, and Nevada, among other states. The Medicaid-coverage losses are expected to spur dozens of safety-net hospitals to close and are projected to cause 51,000 unnecessary deaths . If Democrats regain the White House, they want to do a lot more: universal child care, prescription-drug-price controls, lowering the Medicare-eligibility age, maybe even Medicare for All. These policies come with costs: $90 billion a year for restoring Medicaid, $20 billion for SNAP, $35 billion for the Obamacare subsidies. To cover them, Democrats are planning on reversing Trump’s tax cuts for rich families and corporations. Yet they are torn on whether and how to pay for new proposals going forward. (Lowering the Medicare-eligibility age to 60 would cost something like $25 billion annually; universal child care, $80 billion; single-payer health care, $2 trillion, offset by the evaporation of private-insurance premiums.) They are also torn on whether to make winnowing the deficit a goal unto itself. In an interview with The Wall Street Journal , Brian Schatz, a Democratic senator from Hawaii, objected to the idea that Democrats should have to worry about the budget when Republicans didn’t: “I don’t think we should play this game where the things we want have to be paid for and the things they want can be put on a credit card.” On the revenue side, Democrats have vowed not to raise taxes on the 97 percent of American households earning less than $400,000 a year. (Trump’s tax cuts have made that vow a lot more expensive.) Democrats are considering further reducing the burden on working-class and middle-income households by expanding the earned-income and child tax credits. They’re also joining in the American public’s rollicking tax revolt, pushing carve-outs for seniors, tipped workers, hourly workers, police officers, public-school teachers, and homeowners. Democrats are promising a whole lot of throw and not asking for a lot of take, in other words. This kind of budgetary posture would have worked when the economy was limping out of the global financial crisis in 2012, or when it screeched to a halt in 2020 because of COVID. It doesn’t really work now that deficits are contributing to excess inflation—as voters let Joe Biden and Kamala Harris know in 2024, and as they informed 132 Republican incumbents earlier this month. Still, Democrats are not totally out of tennis balls. Ending the Iran war, easing immigration restrictions, and eliminating tariffs would blunt price increases or even lower prices without running up the debt, as would requiring the AI hyperscalers to pay for their own water and electricity and land, as would implementing cost controls for utilities, as would continuing to fast-track homebuilding in high-priced communities, as would breaking up corporate monopolies, as would having Washington negotiate prescription-drug prices for the American consumer market. (Heck, why not have it set payment rates for medical procedures and doctor visits too?) Getting the IRS to collect the taxes it is statutorily owed would reduce the deficit without harming the 97 percent. Pulling shut loopholes for and raising marginal tax rates on millionaires and billionaires would do the same. In time, borrowing costs would ease, inflation would cool down, and the affordability crisis would let up, as Americans so desperately want. Maybe then we could finally have the conversation about how important drop it is to fetch .

items.title: ‘It is doable’ – Steven Manteaw backs 100% local gold refining target
items.description: The co-chair of the Ghana Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (GHEITI), Dr Steven Manteaw, says Ghana can achieve its target of refining all artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) gold locally by 2028. He says the ambition is within reach if the country expands its refinery infrastructure and reduces gold smuggling to secure sufficient feedstock. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, Dr Manteaw backed the target outlined in the government’s 2027 budget. But he also called for a clear plan to deliver it. “Well, it is doable, and we need to expand the refinery infrastructure,” he told host Evans Mensah. The budget targets 100% local refining of ASM gold by 2028. Meeting that objective would require processing capacity and a reliable supply to keep refineries operating. Dr Manteaw identified the need to “reduce smuggling and get the feedstock” as a key part of achieving the goal. His confidence also rests on the relative ease of adding value to gold compared with some other minerals. “It is not like the industrial minerals, bauxites, manganese, and the rest; those are a bit difficult.” For him, the opportunity extends beyond processing gold within Ghana. Local refining under LBMA certification could help the country access mainstream markets and secure better export returns. He said this would help the economy and allow Ghana to “get higher values for our gold exports”. That makes certification an important part of the ambition, alongside refinery expansion and measures to reduce smuggling. Despite endorsing the target, Manteaw wants the government to explain how it will turn the budget commitment into results. “Want to see the plan that the government has for achieving that laudable objective.”

items.title: American strategist denies receiving $4.5m for Tinubu interview
items.description: By Nwafor Sunday Polycarp, Online News Editor American political strategist and media personality, Diana London, has denied receiving $4.5 million from the Nigerian government for her recent interview with President Bola Tinubu. London, in a post on her X account on Wednesday night, described the allegation as a smear campaign, insisting that neither the Nigerian government nor anyone else in the country paid her the reported sum. She said her visit to Nigeria was to interview Tinubu for a documentary and to see the country for herself. “I unequivocally deny the claim that Nigeria’s government nor anyone else in Nigeria paid me $4.5 million. I went to Nigeria to interview President Tinubu @officialABAT for parts of a documentary and see Nigeria for myself. “This SMEAR CAMPAIGN can make noise, but can’t change the facts or stop me from speaking the truth,” she wrote. The denial comes amid controversy surrounding her interview with Tinubu at the Presidential Villa, Abuja, on Tuesday, and reports alleging that she was linked to a $4.5 million lobbying arrangement involving the Nigerian government in the United States. Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar had called on the Presidency to clarify whether the interview was connected to the reported lobbying contract and disclose the details of the arrangement. In a statement issued on Wednesday by his Director of Strategic Communication, Phrank Shaibu, Atiku said US filings identified London as a consultant to DCI Group AZ, a firm reportedly engaged by the Nigerian government through Aster Legal. He said the filings indicated that DCI Group received a $4.5 million retainer but maintained that the Presidency should clarify whether the interview formed part of the contract. Atiku demanded the publication of the contract, details of the payment and the release of the full, unedited recording of the interview. He also questioned the nature of the engagement, arguing that the Presidency should establish whether the encounter was an independent journalistic exercise or part of a government-funded publicity arrangement. The former vice president further asked the government to disclose who authorised the payment, the source of the funds and whether public money was involved. The controversy followed London’s earlier social media posts praising the security partnership between Nigeria and the United States under Tinubu and US President Donald Trump. In one of the posts, she described Nigeria as the United States’ greatest ally in Africa, saying the security cooperation between both countries was producing results and could create further economic and trade opportunities. She also expressed appreciation for the opportunity to work with individuals representing Nigeria in efforts to strengthen relations between the Trump administration and the Nigerian government. However, the posts were subsequently deleted, while London restricted access to the comment section of her X account following criticism from Nigerian social media users. The development prompted further questions about her engagement with the Tinubu administration and the reported $4.5 million lobbying arrangement. London’s latest statement is her first direct public response to the allegation that she received the money. Meanwhile, the Presidency has yet to publicly clarify whether her interview with Tinubu was connected to the reported lobbying contract. The post American strategist denies receiving $4.5m for Tinubu interview appeared first on Vanguard News .

24-hour Economy: 33 manufacturers, 12 SOEs and 12 OMCs in operation – Kwakye Ofosu
items.description: The government says its 24-hour Economy programme has attracted 33 manufacturing companies, 12 oil marketing companies and 12 state-owned enterprises, with some public institutions reporting significant increases in employment since extending their operations beyond regular working hours. Minister in charge of Government Communications, Felix Kwakye Ofosu, disclosed this in Parliament during debate on the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy, saying the participating businesses and institutions had begun operating round-the-clock shifts under the initiative. He said the 33 manufacturing firms, all members of the Association of Ghana Industries (AGI), had registered with the 24-hour Economy Secretariat and were running multiple shifts. The oil marketing companies on the programme, he added, controlled a combined 247 retail outlets, while 13 depots and refineries had also adopted round-the-clock operations. Mr Kwakye Ofosu told the House that 12 state-owned enterprises (SOEs) had similarly moved to 24-hour operations, with some reporting additional recruitment as a result. He cited the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA), which he said had employed 1,758 people since introducing its extended services in 2025. The Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA) had also recruited 1,400 workers, while the Ghana Airports Company Limited had added 334 employees. The Ghana Investment Promotion Centre (GIPC), he said, had taken on 95 people. The Minister further pointed to the Ghana Publishing Company Limited, where the programme had helped preserve 100 jobs that were at risk because of excess staffing under the company’s previous operating arrangements. “The Ghana Publishing Company Limited should have sent home 100 people because they were over-staffed in their old operations. Because of the 24-hour economy programme, they are able to retain those 100 people,” he said. Mr Kwakye Ofosu presented the figures as evidence that the initiative was moving beyond policy announcements and attracting participation from businesses and public institutions. His account came after the Minority demanded greater clarity on the programme’s implementation and the extent to which it was delivering jobs and expanding economic activity. He also outlined incentives being offered to participating businesses, including deferred duty payments for companies importing machinery directly linked to the programme. The 24-hour Economy initiative is a flagship government policy intended to encourage businesses to operate in multiple shifts, increase the use of production facilities, expand access to services and create employment. The latest figures provide an indication of the institutions that have signed on, although the overall impact of the programme will depend on whether the expanded operations translate into sustained jobs, higher output and improved productivity.

items.title: DGSN : 34 morts dans 2.275 accidents en une semaine en périmètre urbain
items.description: La Direction générale de la sûreté nationale (DGSN), a fait savoir que 34 personnes ont trouvé la mort et 3.036 autres ont été blessées, dont 131 grièvement, dans 2.275 accidents de la circulation survenus en périmètre urbain durant la semaine allant du 9 au 15 novembre. Ces accidents, précise la DGSN, sont principalement dus, dans l'ordre, à l'inadvertance des conducteurs, au non-respect de la priorité, à l'excès de vitesse, à l'inadvertance des piétons, au non-respect de la distance de sécurité, au changement de direction sans usage du clignotant, à la non maîtrise du véhicule, au non-respect du stop, au changement de direction non autorisé, à la circulation en sens interdit, à la circulation sur la voie gauche, au non-respect du feu rouge, au dépassement défectueux et à la conduite en état d'ébriété. Concernant les opérations de contrôle et de répression en matière de circulation, les services de sûreté ont enregistré 53.126 contraventions, dressé 8.024 procès-verbaux transmis au Parquet et procédé au recouvrement de 45.102 amendes transactionnelles. Les sommes perçues au titre de ces contraventions ont atteint 9.991.800 dirhams, a ajouté le communiqué, faisant état de la mise en fourrière municipale de 5.772 véhicules, de la saisie de 8.024 documents et du retrait de la circulation de 744 véhicules. Conakry : à la 13ᵉ AG annuelle d’ARINWA, Mohamed Diawara rappelle que « le crime ne doit jamais constituer une source d’enrichissement »
items.description: La 13e Assemblée générale annuelle du Réseau inter-agences de recouvrement des avoirs pour l'Afrique de l'Ouest (ARINWA) a été lancée ce mercredi 18 novembre à Conakry, sous la présidence de Ibrahima Sory 2 Tounkara, Garde des Sceaux, Ministre de la Justice et des Droits de l’Homme. Dans son discours d'ouverture empreint d'engagement et de reconnaissance, Mohamed Diawara, le Directeur général de l’AGRASC et président du Comité d’organisation de l’Assemblée a mis en avant l'importance de la coopération internationale dans la lutte contre la criminalité économique et financière, tout en soulignant les ambitions de la Guinée à travers l'organisation de ces assises. À l'ouverture des travaux, le Patron de l’AGRASC a marqué cette cérémonie par un discours qui a mis en lumière les enjeux de cette rencontre et la responsabilité collective des États face aux nouvelles formes de criminalité. Dans sa double casquette de premier responsable de l'AGRASC et de président du comité d'organisation, Mohamed Diawara a exprimé son immense honneur d'accueillir les différentes délégations à Conakry. Il a notamment souligné que leur présence traduit un engagement commun en faveur du renforcement de la coopération internationale. Le DG de l'AGRASC n'a pas manqué de saluer l'accompagnement des plus hautes autorités guinéennes. Il a exprimé sa profonde gratitude au Garde des Sceaux, Ministre de la Justice et des Droits de l'Homme, Ibrahima Sory 2 Tounkara, pour sa présence et son soutien constant dans la préparation de ces assises. Il a également rendu un hommage appuyé au Président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, pour sa vision et sa détermination à promouvoir l'État de droit, renforcer la bonne gouvernance et intensifier la lutte contre la corruption. Une reconnaissance qu'il a étendue au gouvernement dirigé par le Premier ministre Amadou Oury Bah, pour son implication dans la réussite de cette rencontre internationale. Mohamed Diawara défend une réponse collective face à la criminalité financière Au-delà du caractère institutionnel de cette cérémonie d'ouverture, Mohamed Diawara a surtout insisté sur la nécessité d'une mobilisation régionale face aux menaces que représentent la criminalité organisée, la corruption, le blanchiment de capitaux et les flux financiers illicites. Pour lui, ces phénomènes constituent aujourd'hui des obstacles majeurs à la stabilité économique et au développement des États. Leur dimension transnationale impose donc une réponse concertée, aucune nation ne pouvant prétendre les combattre efficacement en agissant seule. « Face à ces phénomènes transnationaux, aucun pays ne peut agir efficacement de manière isolée. Nous l'avons bien compris. C'est pourquoi notre réponse doit être collective, coordonnée et solidaire », a-t-il souligné. Poursuivant ses propos, il souligne que c'est précisément dans cette dynamique que s'inscrit la mission de l'ARINWA : « faciliter les échanges de renseignements, renforcer la confiance entre les institutions, promouvoir une coopération efficace en matière de recouvrement des avoirs d'origine criminelle. À cet égard, la lutte contre la criminalité transnationale organisée, la lutte contre la criminalité financière ne saurait se limiter à la condamnation des auteurs d'infractions. Elle doit également permettre d'identifier, de saisir et de confisquer les profits illicites ». Poursuivant, le Directeur général de l'AGRASC a également rappelé une dimension essentielle de la lutte contre la criminalité financière : la nécessité de ne pas s'arrêter à la condamnation des auteurs d'infractions, mais de s'attaquer également aux ressources financières issues de leurs activités illicites. « Le crime ne doit jamais constituer une source d'enrichissement », a-t-il martelé, résumant ainsi l'un des principes fondamentaux qui guide l'action des agences de recouvrement des avoirs. Une approche qui place l'identification, la saisie et la confiscation des biens d'origine criminelle au cœur des stratégies de lutte contre la criminalité économique et financière. Trois jours de travaux pour renforcer les mécanismes de coopération Durant les trois jours de cette Assemblée générale, les participants auront à examiner plusieurs questions stratégiques pour l'avenir du réseau. Selon Mohamed Diawara, les travaux permettront notamment de : « Dresser le bilan des activités du réseau, de partager les meilleures pratiques, d’examiner les cas de coopération internationale et d’aborder la question essentielle de l’affectation des produits des avoirs confisqués. Le recouvrement des avoirs doit en effet contribuer à la réparation des préjudices et, conformément aux législations nationales, au financement d’actions d’intérêt général. Nos échanges permettront également de définir les priorités du réseau pour l’année 2027 ». Pour la Guinée, l'accueil de cette 13e Assemblée générale représente, selon Mohamed Diawara, un honneur, mais également une occasion importante de renforcer les relations entre l'AGRASC, ses homologues de la sous-région et les partenaires internationaux. Une reconnaissance aux partenaires et un engagement pour des résultats concrets Conscient de l'importance de l'accompagnement technique et financier dans la réussite d'une telle rencontre, Mohamed Diawara a tenu à adresser ses remerciements au président et au secrétaire permanent de l'ARINWA, à l'Office des Nations unies contre la drogue et le crime (ONUDC), à la coopération allemande à travers la GIZ, aux projets SecFin Africa, ainsi qu'à l'ensemble des partenaires techniques et financiers. Il a également salué la présence de Ziaba, avant de réaffirmer la disponibilité de l'AGRASC et du comité d'organisation à accompagner les participants durant leur séjour dans la capitale guinéenne. En formulant le vœu de voir ces travaux déboucher sur des recommandations concrètes, le Directeur général de l'AGRASC a ainsi donné le ton d'une Assemblée générale qu'il souhaite décisive pour l'avenir du réseau. « Puisse cette 13e Assemblée générale marquer une nouvelle étape dans la consolidation d'ARINWA et le renforcement de la coopération régionale contre la criminalité économique et financière », a-t-il conclu. À travers cette rencontre, Mohamed Diawara entend ainsi contribuer au renforcement du positionnement de la Guinée dans les mécanismes régionaux de lutte contre les flux financiers illicites. Un rendez-vous qui place la coopération, la mutualisation des expériences et l'efficacité du recouvrement des avoirs criminels au centre des priorités. items.title: Industrie de défense : 40 % des besoins des FAR couverts en 2035
items.description: Portée par l’« Offre Maroc » présentée devant le Roi Mohammed VI, la feuille de route des industries de défense et de sécurité vise à couvrir environ 40 % des besoins des FAR et des organes de sécurité à l’horizon 2035, tout en réalisant plus de 65 % de son chiffre d’affaires à l’export. Couvrir environ 40 % des besoins des Forces Armées Royales et des organes de sécurité par une production nationale : tel est l’un des objectifs fixés à l’horizon 2035 par la feuille de route de l’industrie de défense et de sécurité, présentée ce mercredi 18 novembre au Palais Royal de Rabat. La séance de travail, consacrée à l’« Offre Maroc », a été présidée par le Roi Mohammed VI, accompagné du Prince Héritier Moulay El Hassan, comme l’indique un communiqué du Cabinet Royal. L’exposé a été présenté devant le Souverain par le Général de Corps d’Armée, Inspecteur Général des FAR et Commandant la Zone Sud, et par le Directeur général de l’Agence Marocaine de Développement des Investissements et des Exportations. Les documents de présentation qualifient l’initiative d’« Initiative Royale Structurante ». Elle ambitionne de faire émerger une industrie de défense souveraine, compétitive et tournée vers l’international, appelée à devenir un nouveau moteur de croissance, d’innovation et de création de valeur pour l’économie nationale. Elle s’inscrit dans les Hautes Orientations Royales, qui érigent la souveraineté nationale et l’autonomie stratégique en priorités fondamentales. La couverture de 40 % des besoins nationaux n’est pas le seul objectif chiffré. À la même échéance, la filière doit réaliser plus de 65 % de son chiffre d’affaires à l’exportation, et créer près de 50.000 emplois directs et indirects. Les deux logiques sont censées aller de pair : satisfaire d’abord les besoins du pays, puis conquérir des marchés extérieurs. Les segments visés sont les drones et systèmes autonomes, les systèmes terrestres, les systèmes navals, l’électronique de défense, la cyberdéfense et l’intelligence artificielle, avec une priorité donnée aux complémentarités industrielles et aux usages duals. Cette trajectoire s’appuie sur une base déjà amorcée. Depuis 2020, le Maroc a constitué un premier noyau industriel de défense : véhicules blindés WhAP 8×8 à Berrechid, tourelles de 30 mm pour ces blindés à Midparc Nouaceur, munitions de moyen et gros calibre à Sidi Yahya, fabrication et maintenance de drones militaires à Benslimane, ainsi que R&D, fabrication et intégration de systèmes autonomes et anti-drones. La feuille de route doit permettre de franchir un nouveau palier en capitalisant sur ces projets, sur l’expertise des FAR et sur les acquis du Royaume dans l’aéronautique, l’automobile et l’électronique. Quatre finalités sont assignées à l’initiative. Elle vise d’abord un écosystème industriel intégré, couvrant progressivement toute la chaîne de valeur, de la recherche et développement à la production, l’intégration, la maintenance, les essais et le stockage. Elle entend ensuite renforcer la souveraineté industrielle et technologique, puis ouvrir de nouveaux relais de croissance et de progrès social, grâce à l’investissement, aux compétences avancées, à un tissu de fournisseurs nationaux et à des emplois qualifiés et durables. Elle doit enfin doter le Royaume d’un levier de rayonnement, l’industrie de défense devenant un instrument de diplomatie économique, de coopération industrielle et de partenariats stratégiques et sécuritaires. La mise en œuvre reposera sur une gouvernance dédiée : une agence stratégique, chargée d’appliquer la stratégie nationale et d’accompagner les investisseurs, et une holding industrielle, destinée à structurer les écosystèmes de défense et de sécurité, à mobiliser capitaux publics et privés et à favoriser l’émergence de champions locaux. Deux zones d’accélération industrielle de défense ont déjà été lancées. L’« Offre Maroc » en prévoit deux autres : une zone de grande envergure à Benguérir et une à Benslimane. Le Roi s’est informé de l’avancement des premières zones, des projets engagés et des investisseurs intéressés par une implantation dans le Royaume, notamment pour l’export. Le volet humain n’est pas oublié. Une académie spécialisée dispensera des formations de pointe avec les opérateurs industriels, tandis que les expertises civiles et militaires nationales, ainsi que celles de la Communauté marocaine à l’étranger, seront mobilisées au service de la recherche et de l’innovation. L’« Offre Maroc » s’appuiera aussi sur les partenariats stratégiques privilégiés du Royaume pour renforcer son insertion dans les chaînes de valeur mondiales et ses capacités d’exportation. La base industrielle et technologique de défense est ainsi présentée comme un pilier de la résilience stratégique du Royaume et une plateforme d’approvisionnement et d’exportation fiable. Au terme de la séance, le Souverain a ordonné la mise en œuvre rapide et effective de la feuille de route, en commençant par la mise en place des organes de gouvernance et du plan de financement, en facilitant les procédures d’investissement et en mobilisant le secteur privé national. Il a également insisté sur la mobilisation des compétences nationales, au Maroc et à l’étranger, à travers un programme dédié à l’orientation précoce des jeunes talents et au développement de la formation professionnelle. Le Fonds Hassan II pour le développement économique et social contribuera à hauteur de 4 milliards de dirhams. items.title: Jared Kushner’s Undisclosed Investment
items.description: Jared Kushner was incensed. On October 1, CNN had published an investigative report suggesting that he was profiting from the war in Gaza even as he was serving as a U.S. mediator working to resolve the conflict. Kushner’s private-equity firm, Affinity Partners, was the largest shareholder in an Israeli company called Phoenix Financial, which CNN journalists found had stakes totaling hundreds of millions of dollars in nine Israeli defense contractors. All nine companies saw their stock values rise last year, according to the news network, and many of them credited the Gaza war with boosting demand for their products. In a set of lengthy internet posts , Kushner assailed the CNN report—and the conflicts of interest it accused him of—as unfair. Affinity Partners had made its first, $129 million investment in Phoenix in July 2024, four months before President Trump was reelected and half a year before Kushner returned to public service, at Trump’s behest, as a volunteer peace envoy, trying to negotiate settlements in the Middle East and Ukraine. Kushner stressed that he had no control over Phoenix’s investment choices—he called Phoenix “the Israeli equivalent of Vanguard or Fidelity,” companies that manage many investments—and that neither he nor Affinity owned any of the defense contractors directly. “Misleading stories,” he said on X, “will not distract me from the work President Trump asked me to do: help end wars, bring people together and pursue peace.” Unmentioned in any of Kushner’s posts, however, was that Affinity also owned a $32 million stake in a sprawling American defense contractor—a stake purchased after Trump’s reelection and Kushner’s return to public service but not disclosed until November 5, two days after the midterms, when Affinity belatedly updated a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing, which has not been previously reported, revealed that Affinity had acquired 689,411 shares in a Connecticut-based company, called Arxis, that makes “mission-critical” components for F-35 fighter jets, Navy destroyers, nuclear submarines, and anti-missile systems, most of which have been deployed in the Middle East or Russia-Ukraine theaters in which Kushner has acted as a key negotiator. [ From the January 2027 issue: How Jared Kushner sparked a revolution in the Balkans ] Arxis comprises more than 30 aerospace and defense companies that were joined under a single umbrella and taken public this past April. In SEC filings this year, Arxis emphasized its dependence on the U.S. government for revenue, regulatory approvals, export controls, and security clearances. “The current administration is prioritizing investment in high-tech platforms including those already supported by Arxis (e.g., F-35 Joint Strike Fighter, DDG-51 destroyers, Virginia-class submarines and Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared satellites),” Arxis said in the prospectus for its initial public offering. Of the company’s $1.6 billion in revenue last year, some 47 percent came from defense and space spending. “We generate a significant portion of our revenue from suppliers and contractors for the U.S. government, particularly the Department of War,” Arxis said in its latest quarterly report. It also sells high-end components for military equipment directly to the U.S. government, and to foreign governments and their suppliers. The future, Arxis said in the prospectus, looked bright: “Ongoing global conflicts, coupled with the potential for future conflicts, have accelerated global defense investments.” U.S. military spending was projected to “reach $1 trillion by the fiscal year ended September 30, 2026, a substantial increase” over prior years that the company said was “driven by multi-theater conflicts and a more advanced and complex threat environment,” as well as “rising geopolitical tensions.” War, in short, had been good for business. Arxis lost money in 2023 and 2024, according to its SEC filings, but turned profitable in 2025, the year Trump returned to office. Since going public in April, Arxis has seen its stock price rise by about 60 percent, peaking in early August before declining slightly. “In defense and space, we continue to benefit from our alignment to key government-spending priorities,” Kevin Perhamus, Arxis’s CEO, said in an earnings call this year. When a stock analyst asked for details, Perhamus said, “that’s air defense, radar, missile systems, missile-defense electronics, electronic warfare, modernization. You know, all of the priorities, the key government priorities that exist, we are broadly tied to and always have been.” Under SEC rules, investment managers, such as Affinity, that own more than $100 million in certain kinds of public securities must disclose those holdings within 45 days of each quarter. But in mid-August, when Affinity filed its required paperwork, known as an SEC Form 13F, for the second quarter of 2026, the form made no mention of Arxis, even though Affinity had already acquired its shares in the company by then. The only shares it disclosed on the August form were $565 million worth of stock in a building-supplies company called QXO. Not until November 5—nearly three months after the August filing—did Affinity amend the form. The amendment declared the $32 million investment in Arxis as an omission from its second-quarter report, without explanation. Neither Kushner nor the communications staff at Affinity Partners replied to repeated requests for comment by email, text, and phone today. Kushner, Trump’s billionaire son-in-law, has been dogged for a decade by accusations of too freely mixing private and public business, first by failing to fully divest from his family’s real-estate empire and more recently as the owner of Affinity, which he founded in 2021. Kushner capitalized on relationships he built as a Middle East envoy during Trump’s first administration to raise as much as $6 billion for Affinity, the better part of it from sovereign-wealth funds in the same Gulf states he now deals with as a peace negotiator. [ Read: Jared Kushner’s mysterious role in the Trump administration ] Affinity has invested the funds it has raised in a variety of international businesses, including an online-classifieds company in the United Arab Emirates, a Brazilian fast-food chain, and the American video-game maker Electronic Arts. Arxis appears to be its first direct investment in the defense industry, a major departure from its other ventures, ripe with potential conflicts. As a commander in chief with little regard for bureaucracy or the will of Congress, Kushner’s father-in-law has broad power over military spending. Kushner, meanwhile, is mediating multiple global conflicts—Iran, Ukraine, Gaza—whose duration and outcomes bear directly on the defense industry. Had Affinity disclosed its Arxis stake before the election—and had reporters picked up on it—it would have lent support to a spate of recent stories about Kushner’s alleged conflicts, including the CNN report, a New Yorker article from September, and a controversial book , published in late October, that claims that Kushner had access to secret bank accounts funded by the rulers of Saudi Arabia and the UAE. ( He denies the book’s claim .) It would have also undercut his responses to the coverage, which included an uncharacteristically large number of social - media posts , denials , and counteraccusations from the usually reticent Kushner. His outpouring of indignation now seems to have taken place during a period in which he owned, but failed to disclose, a $32 million stake in an American defense company dependent on the government he served, and on the status of conflicts he was mediating, for a substantial portion of its revenues. Was Kushner worried about how news of the investment might affect the midterms? It wouldn’t have been surprising. Democrats in Congress had named him among the top Trump-world figures they planned to investigate should they retake the majority. As the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have dragged on, Kushner’s interest in the defense industry appears to be growing. On November 12, a week after Affinity reported its stake in Arxis, another company announced Kushner’s firm as a new investor. The company, Q-Ctrl, sells a novel navigation technology sought by the U.S. military because it lacks the vulnerabilities of satellite-based systems such as GPS, which enemies can jam, spoof, or block—a problem endemic in recent conflicts. Last year, Q-Ctrl won a $24.4 million contract from DARPA, the Defense Department’s advanced-research arm, and a joint award, with Lockheed Martin, from the department’s Defense Innovation Unit. Among Q-Ctrl’s other investors is In-Q-Tel, a government-funded nonprofit created by the CIA to identify and develop new tech for intelligence and national security. Before founding Affinity, Kushner had no substantive experience in private equity. One of the questions he’s faced is why nearly all of the money that Affinity has raised comes from Gulf royals with an existential stake in the results of his diplomacy. He now faces a new question: Why would a man working for peace be seeking to profit from war?

items.title: Zverev to defend himself against fresh lawsuit
items.description: Lawyers for world number one Alexander Zverev say he will defend himself against a lawsuit which alleges he misrepresented the outcome of his domestic abuse trial. Former partner Brenda Patea is seeking damages and an injunction to stop him from making similar comments in the future. In October 2023, Zverev was issued with a penalty order for bodily harm against Patea, with whom he has a daughter. He contested the order, having always denied the charges, and a public trial was under way in Berlin in June 2024 when the court terminated the proceedings. “The decision is not a verdict, and it is not a decision about guilt or innocence,” the court told the BBC. “One decisive factor for the decision was that the witness has expressed her wish to end the trial. The defendant agreed to the termination of the case.” The court said Zverev and Patea had reached a separate settlement. But in September, as first reported by the Bounces website, Patea’s lawyers filed a civil complaint in Berlin over an interview Zverev gave to French newspaper L’Equipe in June, the day after he won his first Grand Slam title at Roland Garros. According to the complaint, L’Equipe reported that Zverev allegedly said: “my innocence has been proven”. The lawsuit asks that Zverev should be ordered “on pain of a fine of up to 250,000 euros (£209,000)” not to repeat the claim, and also seeks damages for the impact these statements have made on Patea. “He was not found guilty, but he was not acquitted and they signed an agreement in which he committed not to talk about this case any more,” Patea’s lawyer Michael Scheele told BBC Sport. “Instead he has said that it has been proven that he was not guilty. It’s simply false. “She doesn’t want this to be repeated, because she’s a content creator, an influencer, and she was accused of trying to make money, which was not true. If that had been the case, she would have asked in that [original] agreement to be compensated. “He made a payment for the daughter, but nothing for her. She did not get any money.” Zverev is being represented by Berlin law firm Schertz Bergmann, which said: “Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. “If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law. “Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. “He is fully entitled to hold and express this view. “The criminal proceedings were discontinued without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected.” The out-of-court settlement in Berlin in June 2024 came on the day Zverev reached the French Open final for the first time. At the subsequent news conference, BBC Sport asked whether he had any reservations about missing the chance to clear his name entirely. “That’s what dropping the case is. That is innocence,” Zverev replied. “They’re not going to drop the case if you’re guilty. I don’t know what translations you have, but that’s what it means. “Done. We move on. I never ever want to hear another question about the subject again. That goes out to everybody.”

items.title: Sudan: Transfer War Crimes Suspects to ICC
items.description: Click to expand Image Left to right: Governor of South Kordofan Ahmed Haroun in South Kordofan State, August 23, 2011. © 2011 Reuters; Abdel Rahim Mohammed Hussein. © 2010 غيداء نجم الدين سعيد ابراهيم/Wikipedia; and Omar al-Bashir. © 2009 U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Jesse B. Awalt/Wikipedia (The Hague) – Sudanese authorities should immediately transfer former Interior Minister Ahmed Haroun to the International Criminal Court (ICC) to face charges in The Hague, Human Rights Watch said today. Haroun was recently taken into Sudanese custody and faces ICC war crimes and crimes against humanity charges, committed in Sudan’s Darfur region, in 2003 and 2004. On November 8, 2026, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) reportedly re-arrested Haroun, interior minister of Sudan in 2007, when an ICC arrest warrant was issued against him. He was arrested one day after he took part in a video podcast interview, his first public appearance since 2019. The armed forces have not officially confirmed Haroun’s whereabouts, but media reported that he is detained in Khartoum state. “For two decades, victims of atrocity crimes in Darfur have witnessed Haroun and others evading justice, leading to impunity-fueled cycles of violence that are claiming more victims every day.” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “If Sudan’s authorities transferred those sought by the ICC to the court in The Hague, as they are obliged to do, it would send a powerful message to those committing crimes today that they too may find themselves in the dock.” Authorities should also transfer former President Omar al-Bashir—who is believed to be in Sudanese custody in Khartoum state as well—and locate, arrest, and transfer former Defense Minister Abdelrahim M. Hussein. The ICC has also issued arrest warrants for both of them, though there is no information available on Hussein’s location. The ICC issued an arrest warrant against Haroun in 2007, and another against Hussein in 2012, for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Darfur between 2003 and 2004. During that period, Sudanese government forces and allied militias carried out targeted attacks against civilians on the basis of their ethnicity, including killings, rape, forced displacement from their homes and land, and burning of their villages. In 2009 and 2010, the ICC issued two arrest warrants against al-Bashir for alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide committed in Darfur between 2003 and 2008. Following al-Bashir’s ouster in April 2019, Sudanese authorities held Haroun, al-Bashir, and Hussein in custody for charges not related to atrocities in Darfur but failed to transfer them to the ICC. After fighting erupted between SAF and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on April 15, 2023, the authorities moved al-Bashir to Alia military hospital in Omdurman, Khartoum state, where he reportedly remained under guard, while Haroun left detention amid the collapse of prison security, and under circumstances suggesting coordination with judicial authorities. On September 30, 2026, SAF granted al-Bashir initial approval to travel outside of Sudan for medical treatment. Based on media reports, al-Bashir continues to receive medical care at Alia military hospital and is yet to travel abroad. UN Security Council Resolution 1593, referring the situation in Darfur to the ICC prosecutor, requires the government of Sudan to cooperate with the court even though it is not a party to the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty. In 2021, the ICC’s Office of the Prosecutor signed a memorandum of understanding with the Sudanese authorities addressing cooperation for arrests. The ICC lacks the ability to enforce its own orders and relies on state cooperation to conduct investigations and make arrests. In January and July, the Office of the Prosecutor reported to the United Nations Security Council on its investigation in Darfur, including its continued engagement with Sudanese authorities. In addition to addressing crimes from July 2002 onward, the Office of the Prosecutor is also investigating crimes committed since April 2023 in Darfur. The prosecutor’s office reported “positive” and “significant” cooperation by Sudanese authorities, and assistance in support of its investigative activities, including deployment of the office’s investigative team to Port Sudan. Nevertheless, Sudan has not fulfilled its obligation to carry out the court’s arrest warrants and transfer the wanted suspects to the Hague. The authorities should provide public information on the whereabouts of all the wanted suspects and take immediate steps to allow their transfer to the court, Human Rights Watch said. The African Union, the members of the Atrocity Prevention and Justice Coalition for Sudan–– particularly the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Sierra Leone––as well as the European Union and its member states should directly engage with Sudanese authorities, calling on them to comply with their obligation to fully cooperate with the ICC and to transfer Haroun, al-Bashir, and Hussein to the court’s custody. ICC judges have referred to the Security Council several findings of noncooperation against Sudan and ICC member states in relation to the arrest of ICC suspects. However, the council has never taken steps to enforce these findings. UN member states should urge the Security Council to back the ICC’s mandate in Darfur, including by enforcing the court’s findings of noncooperation on arrests. The ICC prosecutor’s office should use its next biannual report to the council, in January 2027, as an opportunity to raise any concerns related to Sudan’s cooperation on arrests. In 2025, the ICC convicted Ali Muhammad Ali Abd-Al-Rahman (also known as Ali Kosheib), a former leader of Sudan’s “Janjaweed” militias, for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur in 2003 and 2004, and sentenced him to 20 years in prison. Kosheib’s trial was possible after he surrendered himself voluntarily to the ICC’s custody in 2020. “For victims and survivors of crimes in Darfur, Sudanese authorities’ promises of cooperation mean little without concrete action,” Evenson said. “Sudan’s international partners should use every diplomatic tool at their disposal to press for the immediate transfer of all ICC suspects in Sudanese custody and make clear that cooperation with the court is not optional.”

items.title: Les Forces armées à l’honneur ce 19 novembre
items.description: Au cours du conseil des ministres , le président de la République a également annoncé qu’il présidera, ce jeudi 19 novembre 2026, au quartier Dial Diop, la Journée des Forces armées. Placée sous le thème « Forces armées, vecteurs de l’intégration sous-régionale et de la sécurité collective », cette célébration s’inscrit, selon le communiqué, en cohérence avec la présidence en exercice du Sénégal à la tête de la CEDEAO. Le chef de l’État a adressé ses félicitations aux Forces armées pour leur engagement, leur professionnalisme et leur exemplarité, qui contribuent au renforcement de la sécurité nationale et sous-régionale ainsi qu’au rayonnement international du Sénégal. En sa qualité de chef suprême des Armées, il a réaffirmé sa volonté d'améliorer la condition militaire, de renforcer les équipements et de poursuivre la modernisation des forces de défense et de sécurité, dans un environnement international marqué par de nombreux défis sécuritaires et technologiques. Un agenda présidentiel chargé Le président de la République est également revenu sur ses récentes activités diplomatiques, notamment sa participation au Forum de Paris sur la Paix, les 10 et 11 novembre, ainsi qu’au 20e Sommet de la Francophonie, tenu du 14 au 16 novembre à Phnom Penh, au Cambodge. Son agenda des prochains jours sera marqué par plusieurs rendez-vous. Après la Journée des Forces armées et la cérémonie d’ouverture de la Biennale de l’Art africain contemporain, prévues ce 19 novembre, il recevra, le lendemain, les médaillés, le mouvement olympique et les acteurs culturels ayant contribué à l’organisation des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026. Le chef de l’État a, en outre, annoncé une tournée économique dans les régions de Tambacounda et de Kédougou, du 26 au 29 novembre. Celle-ci sera suivie de la commémoration de la Journée des Tirailleurs, le 1er décembre, puis de l’inauguration de l’usine de dessalement d’eau de mer des Mamelles, prévue le 3 décembre 2026.

items.title: Migration irrégulière :Le chef de l’État réclame un nouveau plan d’action
items.description: Face à la recrudescence des départs vers l’Europe et au drame survenu à Lompoul, le président de la République demande au gouvernement de renforcer les contrôles sur les côtes et de proposer un programme spécial d’insertion et d’entrepreneuriat des jeunes. Il a également instruit le Premier ministre de tenir une réunion consacrée à cette problématique lors du traditionnel conseil des ministres. La lutte contre la migration irrégulière doit prendre un nouvel élan. Face à la recrudescence et à l’intensification des départs de migrants vers l’Europe, le président de la République appelle à un renforcement des dispositifs de contrôle sur les côtes sénégalaises et à la mise en œuvre de mesures gouvernementales urgentes. Cette préoccupation a été soulevée lors du Conseil des ministres de ce mercredi 18 novembre 2026. À la suite de la tragédie de Lompoul, le chef de l’État s’est incliné devant la mémoire des personnes décédées ou portées disparues en mer, tout en présentant les condoléances de la Nation aux familles endeuillées. Il a, dans le même temps, demandé au ministre de l’Intérieur et de la Sécurité publique de lui soumettre un rapport circonstancié sur les problématiques liées à la migration irrégulière, ainsi que sur les solutions concertées et adaptées à apporter. Ce rapport devra également dresser le bilan de la stratégie et des actions conduites dans le cadre du Comité interministériel de lutte contre la migration irrégulière (CILMI). Au-delà des mesures sécuritaires, le président de la République estime que la complexité du phénomène impose une réponse structurelle, articulée autour de l’emploi et de l’insertion socio-économique. Il préconise ainsi une accélération des politiques publiques dans les domaines de la jeunesse, de l’éducation, de la formation professionnelle et de l’emploi, mais aussi de l’entrepreneuriat des jeunes et de l’autonomisation économique des femmes. Le chef de l’État insiste également sur la relance des secteurs de l’Agriculture et des Pêches, considérés comme des leviers importants dans la lutte contre le phénomène. Il demande, par ailleurs, d’accélérer le déploiement des dispositifs publics ciblés, dans le cadre d’un nouveau Programme prioritaire d’insertion et de promotion de l’entrepreneuriat des jeunes. Le Premier ministre est ainsi chargé de tenir une réunion sur cette question et de lui transmettre des propositions relatives à un programme spécial destiné aux jeunes.

items.title: Alcaraz continues winning run despite injury concern
items.description: Carlos Alcaraz continued his sensational late-season form as he outclassed world number five Daniil Medvedev to reach the knockout stage at the ATP Finals. But the 23-year-old Spaniard later said he had felt “a little problem” with his hamstring. Alcaraz produced another sparkling display to control the contest throughout, despite ending the match with heavy strapping on his upper-left leg. The issue did not disrupt the world number three, who led by a set and a break after treatment, and cruised to a 6-2 6-4 win in just 72 minutes. “Right now I’m just feeling OK,” said Alcaraz, whose semi-final qualification was confirmed by Frances Tiafoe’s win over Flavio Cobolli. “We will see with my team and physio, but I think the rest of today and tomorrow are really going to be important days ahead of me.” It was the seven-time major winner’s 11th consecutive victory, following back-to-back titles at the Vienna Open and Paris Masters. Alcaraz is scheduled to face Italy’s Cobolli, who cannot reach the knockout stage after his 7-6 (8-6) 6-0 loss to Tiafoe, in his final group match in Turin on Friday. Asked what pleased him most about his performance, Alcaraz replied: “Everything”. “We could see in [Medvedev’s] first match that he was serving very well. I returned really well, really aggressively, and really deep,” he added. “I think I just hit the ball in a sweet spot every time. I’m really happy about it.” Given the outstanding levels at which he is currently operating, it is easy to forget that Alcaraz spent four months out of action in the middle of the season. The former world number one’s rapid return from that wrist injury to his scintillating best has been astonishing. Alcaraz has won three titles and lost just twice in 24 matches since making his return at the US Open in August, when his lack of match fitness appeared to catch up with him in a four-and-a-half hour epic against Ben Shelton . Just 10 weeks on, he delivered one of the best indoor performances of his career in sweeping past 2020 champion Medvedev. That came two days after he began his latest bid for a first ATP Finals title with a statement victory over Tiafoe – and later warned his rivals he has never felt better at this stage of the season . Medvedev beat home hope Cobolli in straight sets in his opening match for his first win against a top-10 opponent since defeating Alcaraz at Indian Wells in March. The Russian was no match for the Australian Open champion on this occasion, however. A dominant seven-game streak ultimately decided the match, as Alcaraz ran away with the first set and then broke immediately in the second to take firm control. The second seed did not face a single break point as he outmanoeuvred Medvedev, firing 16 winners and committing just 13 unforced errors. It was a display which scored 9.5 out of 10 on the ATP’s performance rating, which combines several statistics to measure a player’s overall game, following a 9.6 in his opener. That was despite Alcaraz playing the final seven games with a hamstring issue, which he will now work to overcome in the next 48 hours. Tiafoe keeps semi-final hopes alive Frances Tiafoe claimed his sixth win against top-10 opponents in 2026 – the third-most on the tour behind Jannik Sinner (10) and Carlos Alcaraz (eight) Tiafoe will go head-to-head with Medvedev for a place in the semi-finals after earning his first career win over home favourite Cobolli at the ATP Finals. The importance of this match to both players’ aspirations of progressing on their tournament debut was evident in a tense opening set with several momentum swings. But it was Tiafoe, 28, who managed to maintain his composure in key moments, the American world number eight recovering from 3-1 and a break point down in the set, and two set points down at 6-4 in the tie-break, to take control of the match. Cobolli’s frustration was clear as he missed significant opportunities on Tiafoe’s serve to lead 4-1 and 5-4, before conceding the tie-break after losing four consecutive points. With Cobolli unable to shake off that disappointment, Tiafoe cruised to victory by winning 28 of the 40 points played in a one-sided second set to book a winner-takes-all meeting with Medvedev. In the doubles, Briton Neal Skupski and American teammate Christian Harrison, seeded second on their tournament debut in Italy, bounced back from their opening defeat with a 6-3 6-4 victory over Italians Simone Bolelli and Andrea Vavassori.

items.title: Belize: Los países del MIRPS reafirman su compromiso con el fortalecimiento de los sistemas de protección, la promoción de soluciones duraderas y la generación de oportunidades de inclusión para personas con necesidades de protección
items.description: Countries: Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Panama Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees SAN SALVADOR – Los siete países que integran el Marco Integral Regional para la Protección y Soluciones (MIRPS) –Belice, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, México y Panamá– concluyeron hoy la IX Reunión Anual del MIRPS con la adopción de la Declaración de San Salvador II , mediante la cual renovaron sus compromisos para fortalecer los sistemas nacionales de protección, ampliar las oportunidades de inclusión socioeconómica y avanzar en soluciones duraderas para personas con necesidades de protección y las comunidades que las acogen. Durante el encuentro, celebrado bajo el liderazgo del Gobierno de El Salvador en su calidad de Presidencia Pro-Témpore 2026, autoridades de los países MIRPS, representantes de la Plataforma de Apoyo y socios estratégicos realizaron un balance de los avances alcanzados durante 2026 y examinaron las oportunidades y las prioridades que orientarán la cooperación regional en 2027. El diálogo destacó los resultados y buenas prácticas en materia de asilo, protección a nivel territorial, gobernabilidad local y medios de vida. La Reunión Anual culminó con la adopción de la Declaración de San Salvador II, en la que los Estados acordaron promover procedimientos de asilo más accesibles, eficientes y de calidad, ampliar el acceso a empleo, educación y medios de vida, e incorporar enfoques de protección en las políticas de gestión del riesgo de desastres y adaptación al cambio climático. Los países también destacaron la importancia de profundizar la cooperación con otros mecanismos regionales y fortalecer las alianzas con gobiernos locales, sociedad civil, organizaciones lideradas por personas refugiadas, academia, sector privado y actores del desarrollo, con el propósito de ampliar el alcance y la sostenibilidad de las respuestas. Asimismo, reconocieron el valor del MIRPS como una plataforma regional que permite promover respuestas coordinadas en beneficio de las personas con necesidades de protección y las comunidades de acogida. La Organización de los Estados Americanos (OEA), que integra junto con ACNUR la Secretaría Técnica del MIRPS, destacó los avances del Fondo MIRPS, cuyos proyectos han beneficiado a más de 33.000 personas en la región, y agradeció las contribuciones de España, la República de Corea y Portugal. “El desplazamiento sigue afectando a personas y familias en todo nuestro hemisferio. Atender sus necesidades va más allá de brindar protección inmediata y requiere instituciones sólidas, políticas inclusivas y una cooperación regional que abra caminos hacia la estabilidad y las oportunidades. Estos principios guían la Agenda de Paz y Prosperidad para las Américas de la OEA. En nuestro trabajo con las personas desplazadas, esto significa acceso a la protección, la documentación, la educación y el empleo, así como oportunidades para desarrollar su autonomía y vivir con dignidad”, afirmó Albert R. Ramdin, Secretario General de la OEA, al destacar el compromiso de la Organización con la protección y la inclusión de las personas con necesidades de protección. En el marco del 75.º aniversario de la Convención sobre el Estatuto de los Refugiados de 1951, ACNUR destacó la importancia de mantener el compromiso regional con la protección internacional. “La adopción de la Declaración de San Salvador II demuestra que los países de la región siguen apostando por la cooperación, la solidaridad y la responsabilidad compartida para responder al desplazamiento. A través del MIRPS, los Estados continúan transformando sus compromisos en acciones concretas para las personas refugiadas, desplazadas y las comunidades que las acogen", afirmó Isabel Márquez, Directora Regional de ACNUR para las Américas. Los miembros de la Plataforma de Apoyo al MIRPS reafirmaron su compromiso de continuar acompañando los esfuerzos de los países mediante la cooperación técnica, la movilización de recursos y el fortalecimiento de alianzas estratégicas para apoyar la implementación de las prioridades nacionales y regionales, ampliar las oportunidades de protección y soluciones duraderas, y contribuir a la sostenibilidad de los esfuerzos impulsados por los Estados que integran este Mecanismo. Al cierre de la IX Reunión Anual, El Salvador traspasó la Presidencia Pro-Témpore del MIRPS a Guatemala, que liderará el mecanismo durante 2027, en un año particularmente significativo en el que el MIRPS conmemorará su décimo aniversario. A una década de la adopción de la Declaración de San Pedro Sula, este Mecanismo continúa consolidándose como una plataforma regional de cooperación, innovación y responsabilidad compartida que permite a los Estados avanzar conjuntamente en la protección, la inclusión y las soluciones para las personas refugiadas, desplazadas y otras personas con necesidades de protección internacional. El Marco Integral Regional para la Protección y Soluciones (MIRPS) está integrado por Belice, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, México y Panamá. Es un mecanismo regional para la aplicación del Pacto Mundial sobre los Refugiados que promueve la cooperación y la responsabilidad compartida en materia de prevención, protección y soluciones duraderas frente al desplazamiento. La Plataforma de Apoyo al MIRPS, creada en 2019, contribuye a movilizar recursos y cooperación internacional. ACNUR y la OEA, a través de su Departamento de Acceso a Derechos (DAR), integran la Secretaría Técnica del MIRPS y su Plataforma de Apoyo. Para más información sobre este tema, favor de contactar: En ACNUR: Melanie Gallant, gallant@unhcr.org En la OEA: Nicole Levoyer, NLevoyer@oas.org

items.title: English FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on
items.description: The English Football Association has considered challenging Gianni Infantino’s eligibility to run for a fourth term as FIFA president, BBC Sport can reveal. But it believes any attempt to prevent him from standing in the March election is likely to fail. Infantino introduced a three-term limit when he replaced Sepp Blatter as leader of world football’s governing body. However, Fifa’s council agreed in 2022 that his first term in office, from 2016 to 2019, should not count because it covered the remainder of his predecessor’s interrupted final term. Earlier this month, human rights campaign group Fair Square wrote to the FA, claiming the decision is open to legal challenge and “contrary to the spirit and purpose” of FIFA statutes. It urged the FA to ask FIFA’s governance committee to bar Infantino from the March election because he has already served the maximum three terms. FA chair Debbie Hewitt has now replied, telling Fair Square that the governing body “has explored the possibility of challenging Mr Infantino’s eligibility to run for a further term as the Fifa president but does not consider that such a challenge would secure the outcome sought”. In correspondence seen by the BBC, Hewitt adds: “Ultimately the process followed FIFA’s governance and led to an outcome where Mr Infantino’s part-term was disregarded for the purposes of maximum term limits. “Having considered the process in detail, we do not believe that a challenge would succeed.” In a statement, Fair Square said: “It’s understandable that the FA has no faith in FIFA’s internal processes to hold Infantino accountable for serious breaches of the rules, but it’s a mistake to abandon these channels, not least because it sends a signal to Infantino that he can do whatever he likes. “We will encourage the FA to leave its options open where this matter is concerned, not least because Debbie Hewitt’s position on the Fifa council puts her in a very strong position to demand clear answers on why Fifa discounted Infantino’s first term.” Miguel Maduro – a former head of Fifa’s governance committee – has said a national association or confederation may need to challenge Infantino’s eligibility at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS). However, he also said European football associations have found it harder to do so because UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin decided to stand for a fourth term earlier this year. Ceferin reversed his earlier insistence that he would not seek re-election in 2024. The FA was among several national associations that withdrew their support for Infantino after the crisis sparked by his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors. European confederation UEFA has backed rival candidate Philippe Diallo, the president of the French Football Federation. Hewitt, who joined Fifa’s council in 2023, also told Fair Square that the FA “remains opposed to Mr Infantino’s re-election and is committed to providing its full support to Philippe Diallo as our preferred candidate in the upcoming Fifa presidential election”. FIFA has been approached for comment. It has previously referred to the fact that in 2022 its council “unanimously confirmed its agreement with the view of the governance, audit & compliance committee that the period between 2016 and 2019 does not count as a term of office for the current Fifa president, who is therefore about to end his first term”. The FA declined to comment.

items.title: Biennale de Dakar : le Président de la République présidera l’ouverture de la 16e édition
items.description: Le chef de l’État présidera, jeudi 19 novembre, la cérémonie d’ouverture de la 16e édition de la Biennale de l’Art africain contemporain, prévue jusqu’au 19 décembre.L’annonce a été faite ce mercredi 18 novembre 2026, en Conseil des ministres. La Biennale de Dakar s’impose comme l’un des grands rendez-vous culturels du continent. À l’occasion de sa 16e édition, prévue du 19 novembre au 19 décembre 2026, le Président de la République souligne l’importance de cette manifestation dans le rayonnement culturel du Sénégal. Dans sa communication en Conseil des ministres ce mercredi 18 novembre, le chef de l’État rappelle que la Biennale de l’Art africain contemporain « reste l’une des grandes manifestations culturelles du Continent ». Elle réunira, selon lui, « l’élite culturelle internationale » et consacrera ainsi « la place primordiale du Sénégal dans l’agenda culturel de l’Afrique ». En sa qualité de « premier Protecteur des Arts et des Lettres du Sénégal », le Président de la République adresse ses encouragements et son soutien à l’ensemble des artistes, particulièrement ceux dont les œuvres ont été minutieusement sélectionnées. Il demande, à cet effet, au Premier ministre, au ministre de la Culture, de l’Artisanat et du Tourisme ainsi qu’au ministre chargé de la Culture, des Industries créatives et du Patrimoine historique, de prendre toutes les dispositions nécessaires pour assurer le bon déroulement de la Biennale de Dakar 2026. Le chef de l’État présidera la cérémonie officielle d’ouverture de cette 16e édition, ce jeudi 19 novembre 2026.

items.title: Human Rights Watch Mourns Death of Activist Nabeel Rajab
items.description: Click to expand Image Bahraini human rights activist Nabeel Rajab arrives for his appeal hearing at court in Manama, February 11, 2015. © 2015 Hamad I Mohammed/Reuters (New York) – Nabeel Rajab, a prominent human rights activist from Bahrain and a close partner of Human Rights Watch, passed away on November 17, 2026, at the age of 62. He reportedly died in Türkiye following a heart attack. Rajab rose to prominence as a human rights defender in Bahrain in the 1990s, and in 2000 he co-founded the Bahrain Human Rights Society, one of Bahrain’s first human rights organizations. He then co-founded and later became the president of the Bahrain Centre for Human Rights. Rajab had served as a member of the Human Rights Watch Middle East and North Africa division’s advisory committee since 2010, playing a key role not only in supporting Human Rights Watch work in Bahrain, but also providing guidance to the documentation and advocacy work that Human Rights Watch carries out across the region. Bahraini authorities unjustly detained and imprisoned him several times for his peaceful expression in the years following the 2011 pro-democracy protests in Bahrain. In 2018, he was sentenced to five years in prison for his comments criticizing torture at a Bahraini prison and the Saudi-led military campaign in Yemen. Even from detention, he continued his activism. In 2017, he wrote an op-ed for the New York Times from detention, titled “Don’t Profit from Abuses by Bahrain,” calling out US support of Bahraini authorities despite their abuses both in Bahrain and amid the conflict in Yemen. He wrote: All our destinies are tied together. What will happen to Bahrain if everyone who supports peace, democracy and the rule of law is in jail? To whom will Bahrain’s disenfranchised youth turn to for support and guidance? These are the questions the Trump administration must ask itself before it sends my jailers another batch of fighter jets. He was released from prison in 2020 and allowed to serve the rest of his sentence at home with his family, but only after his health deteriorated due to harsh detention conditions. In the years that followed, he continued to support the human rights movement and call out human rights abuses by Bahraini and other authorities across the world. Sayed Ahmed al-Wadaei, the advocacy director at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy and a close friend, said that Rajab left Bahrain in March 2026 so that he could speak publicly on Bahraini human rights issues. He remained in exile until his passing, unable to return to Bahrain for fear of being rearrested. Rajab’s death is a profound blow to the global and Arab human rights movements, which have lost a steadfast defender of freedom of expression and a voice of reason in a climate increasingly marked by hatred and polarization. Over many years, Rajab stood resolutely by his principles, despite being targeted, detained, and repressed for his unwavering commitment to universal human rights. “Nabeel was a stalwart champion for human rights and democracy, not just for Bahrain but all of the Middle East,” said Sarah Leah Whitson, former Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “He paid a tremendous price for his advocacy, jailed and abused in prison, but always kept us hopeful and resilient. He played an essential role in guiding and supporting the work of Human Rights Watch’s MENA division. I considered him a true friend.” “Nabeel’s legacy lives on in the innumerable people he inspired, fought alongside in the defense of rights, and held up, sometimes in their darkest moments,” said Balkees Jarrah, Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “He has been a leader and guide to human rights defenders in the region. He and his family paid a high price for his activism, but we are grateful for his wisdom, tenacity, and courage.” Nabeel Rajab’s courage, integrity, and principled advocacy will be his enduring legacy. Our thoughts are with his family, loved ones, and the many friends who mourn his loss.
